As to things then which ought to be done and ought not to be done, and good and bad, and beautiful and ugly, all of us talking of them at random go to the philosophers; and on these matters we praise, we censure, we accuse, we blame, we judge and determine about principles honorable and dishonorable. But why do we go to the philosophers? Because we wish to learn what we do not think that we know. And what is this? Theorems. For we wish to learn what philosophers say as being something elegant and acute; and some wish to learn that they may get profit from what they learn. It is ridiculous then to think that a person wishes to learn one thing, and will learn another; or further, that a man will make proficiency in that which he does not learn.
discourses_how-we-must-adapt-preconcepti.plainEnglish:
What's the first job of anyone who wants to study philosophy? Get rid of your ego. You can't learn something you think you already know.

We all talk randomly about what should and shouldn't be done. We debate good and bad, beautiful and ugly. We praise and blame. We judge what's honorable and dishonorable. But then we go to philosophers. Why? Because we want to learn what we don't think we know. And what's that? Abstract theories. We want to learn what philosophers say because it sounds clever and sharp. Some people want to learn so they can profit from it.

It's ridiculous to think you'll learn one thing when you want to learn something else. It's just as ridiculous to think you'll make progress in something you're not actually learning.

discourses_how-we-must-adapt-preconcepti.originalText: But the many are deceived by this which deceived also the rhetorician Theopompus, when he blames even Plato for wishing everything to be defined. For what does he say? Did none of us before you use the words good or just, or do we utter the sounds in an unmeaning and empty way without understanding what they severally signify? Now who tells you, Theopompus, that we had not natural notions of each of these things and preconceptions ([Greek: prolaepseis])? But it is not possible to adapt preconceptions to their correspondent objects if we have not distinguished (analyzed) them, and inquired what object must be subjected to each preconception. You may make the same charge against physicians also. For who among us did not use the words healthy and unhealthy before Hippocrates lived, or did we utter these words as empty sounds? For we have also a certain preconception of health, but we are not able to adapt it. For this reason one says, Abstain from food; another says, Give food; another says, Bleed; and another says, Use cupping. What is the reason? is it any other than that a man cannot properly adapt the preconceptions of health to particulars?
discourses_how-we-must-adapt-preconcepti.plainEnglish: Most people get fooled by the same thing that fooled the speaker Theopompus when he criticized Plato for wanting to define everything. What does Theopompus say? "Did none of us use words like 'good' or 'just' before you came along? Or were we just making empty sounds without knowing what they meant?" But who told you, Theopompus, that we didn't already have natural ideas about these things? We do have basic concepts built into us. But you can't properly use these concepts unless you've thought them through carefully and figured out what each one actually applies to. You could make the same complaint about doctors. Who among us didn't use words like 'healthy' and 'unhealthy' before Hippocrates was around? Were we just making empty sounds? We do have a basic idea of what health means, but we can't apply it properly. That's why one doctor says "Don't eat," another says "Eat more," another says "Bleed the patient," and another says "Use cupping." Why does this happen? Because people can't properly match their basic concepts of health to specific situations.

discourses_how-we-should-struggle-agains.originalText: Every habit and faculty is maintained and increased by the corresponding actions: the habit of walking by walking, the habit of running by running. If you would be a good reader, read; if a writer, write. But when you shall not have read for thirty days in succession, but have done something else, you will know the consequence. In the same way, if you shall have lain down ten days, get up and attempt to make a long walk, and you will see how your legs are weakened. Generally then if you would make anything a habit, do it; if you would not make it a habit, do not do it, but accustom yourself to do something else in place of it.
discourses_how-we-should-struggle-agains.plainEnglish: Every habit and skill gets stronger when you practice it. Walking gets better by walking. Running gets better by running. Want to be a good reader? Read. Want to be a writer? Write. But if you don't read for thirty days straight and do other things instead, you'll see what happens. Same thing if you lie around for ten days. Try to take a long walk after that — you'll see how weak your legs have gotten. So here's the rule: if you want to build a habit, do it. If you don't want that habit, don't do it. Instead, get used to doing something else.

discourses_how-we-should-struggle-agains.originalText: So it is with respect to the affections of the soul: when you have been angry, you must know that not only has this evil befallen you, but that you have also increased the habit, and in a manner thrown fuel upon fire. In this manner certainly, as philosophers say, also diseases of the mind grow up. For when you have once desired money, if reason be applied to lead to a perception of the evil, the desire is stopped, and the ruling faculty of our mind is restored to the original authority. But if you apply no means of cure, it no longer returns to the same state, but being again excited by the corresponding appearance, it is inflamed to desire quicker than before: and when this takes place continually, it is henceforth hardened (made callous), and the disease of the mind confirms the love of money. For he who has had a fever, and has been relieved from it, is not in the same state that he was before, unless he has been completely cured. Something of the kind happens also in diseases of the soul. Certain traces and blisters are left in it, and unless a man shall completely efface them, when he is again lashed on the same places, the lash will produce not blisters (weals) but sores.
discourses_how-we-should-struggle-agains.plainEnglish: The same thing happens with emotions. When you get angry, you need to know that two bad things just happened. First, you got angry. Second, you made the anger habit stronger. You threw fuel on the fire. This is how mental diseases grow, according to philosophers. Say you want money badly. If you use reason to see why this craving is bad, the desire stops. Your mind returns to normal. But if you don't treat it, your mind doesn't go back to how it was. The next time something triggers that same desire, it flares up faster and stronger than before. Keep letting this happen, and the craving hardens into a permanent disease. You become a money-lover. It's like having a fever. Even after the fever breaks, you're not the same as before unless you're completely healed. The same thing happens with diseases of the soul. They leave marks and scars behind. If you don't completely erase these marks, the next time you get hit in the same spot, you won't just get blisters. You'll get open wounds.

discourses_how-we-should-struggle-agains.originalText: If then you wish not to be of an angry temper, do not feed the habit: throw nothing on it which will increase it: at first keep quiet, and count the days on which you have not been angry. I used to be in passion every day; now every second day; then every third, then every fourth. But if you have intermitted thirty days, make a sacrifice to God. For the habit at first begins to be weakened, and then is completely destroyed. "I have not been vexed to-day, nor the day after, nor yet on any succeeding day during two or three months; but I took care when some exciting things happened." Be assured that you are in a good way. How then shall this be done? Be willing at length to be approved by yourself, be willing to appear beautiful to God, desire to be in purity with your own pure self and with God. Then when any such appearance visits you, Plato says, Have recourse to expiations, go a suppliant to the temples of the averting deities. It is even sufficient if you resort to the society of noble and just men, and compare yourself with them, whether you find one who is living or dead.
discourses_how-we-should-struggle-agains.plainEnglish: If you want to stop being angry all the time, don't feed that habit. Don't give it anything that makes it stronger. Start by staying quiet and counting the days you didn't get angry. I used to get angry every day. Then every other day. Then every third day, then every fourth. If you go thirty days without getting angry, make an offering to God. The habit gets weaker at first, then disappears completely. "I haven't been upset today, or yesterday, or for two or three months — even when annoying things happened." Trust me, you're on the right track. How do you do this? Be willing to finally approve of yourself. Be willing to look beautiful to God. Want to be pure with your pure self and with God. Then when anger tries to visit you, Plato says: find ways to cleanse yourself, go pray at temples that turn away bad things. It's enough just to spend time with noble and good people, and compare yourself to them — whether they're alive or dead.

discourses_how-we-should-struggle-agains.originalText: But in the first place, be not hurried away by the rapidity of the appearance, but say, Appearances, wait for me a little; let me see who you are, and what you are about; let me put you to the test. And then do not allow the appearance to lead you on and draw lively pictures of the things which will follow; for if you do, it will carry you off wherever it pleases. But rather bring in to oppose it some other beautiful and noble appearance, and cast out this base appearance. And if you are accustomed to be exercised in this way, you will see what shoulders, what sinews, what strength you have. But now it is only trifling words, and nothing more.
discourses_how-we-should-struggle-agains.plainEnglish: Don't get swept away by first impressions. When something appears in your mind, tell it: "Wait. Let me see what you really are. Let me test you first." Don't let that first impression drag you along and paint vivid pictures of what might happen next. If you do, it will take you wherever it wants. Instead, bring in a better, nobler thought to fight against it. Kick out the bad impression. If you practice this regularly, you'll discover what real strength you have. Right now, you're just talking. Nothing more.

discourses_how-we-should-struggle-agains.originalText: This is the true athlete, the man who exercises himself against such appearances. Stay, wretch, do not be carried away. Great is the combat, divine is the work; it is for kingship, for freedom, for happiness, for freedom from perturbation. Remember God; call on him as a helper and protector, as men at sea call on the Dioscuri in a storm. For what is a greater storm than that which comes from appearances which are violent and drive away the reason? For the storm itself, what else is it but an appearance? For take away the fear of death, and suppose as many thunders and lightnings as you please, and you will know what calm and serenity there is in the ruling faculty. But if you have once been defeated and say that you will conquer hereafter, and then say the same again, be assured that you will at last be in so wretched a condition and so weak that you will not even know afterwards that you are doing wrong, but you will even begin to make apologies (defences) for your wrong-doing, and then you will confirm the saying of Hesiod to be true, With constant ills the dilatory strives.
discourses_how-we-should-struggle-agains.plainEnglish: This is what a true athlete looks like — someone who trains against these mental impressions. Stop right there, you fool. Don't let yourself get swept away. This is a huge fight. The work is sacred. You're fighting for your freedom, your happiness, your peace of mind. Remember God. Call on him to help and protect you, like sailors calling on the gods during a storm. What storm is worse than the one that comes from violent impressions that drive out your reason? The storm itself — what is it but just another impression? Take away your fear of death. Let there be as much thunder and lightning as you want. You'll see how calm and peaceful your mind can be. But if you lose once and say "I'll win next time," and then say it again, know this: you'll end up so miserable and weak that you won't even realize you're doing wrong anymore. You'll start making excuses for your bad behavior. Then you'll prove Hesiod right: "The person who keeps putting things off struggles with constant troubles."

discourses_of-inconsistency.originalText: Some things men readily confess, and other things they do not. No one then will confess that he is a fool or without understanding; but quite the contrary you will hear all men saying, I wish that I had fortune equal to my understanding. But men readily confess that they are timid, and they say: I am rather timid, I confess; but as to other respects you will not find me to be foolish. A man will not readily confess that he is intemperate; and that he is unjust, he will not confess at all. He will by no means confess that he is envious or a busybody. Most men will confess that they are compassionate. What then is the reason?
discourses_of-inconsistency.plainEnglish: People will admit some things about themselves, but not others. No one will admit they're stupid or lack understanding. Instead, you'll hear everyone say, "I wish my luck matched my brains." But people readily admit they're scared. They'll say, "I'm pretty timid, I admit it. But otherwise, you won't find me foolish." A man won't easily admit he lacks self-control. He definitely won't admit he's unfair. He won't admit he's jealous or a meddler. Most people will admit they're caring. So what's going on here?

discourses_of-inconsistency.originalText: The chief thing (the ruling thing) is inconsistency and confusion in the things which relate to good and evil. But different men have different reasons; and generally what they imagine to be base, they do not confess at all. But they suppose timidity to be a characteristic of a good disposition, and compassion also; but silliness to be the absolute characteristic of a slave. And they do not at all admit (confess) the things which are offences against society. But in the case of most errors for this reason chiefly they are induced to confess them, because they imagine that there is something involuntary in them as in timidity and compassion; and if a man confess that he is in any respect intemperate, he alleges love (or passion) as an excuse for what is involuntary. But men do not imagine injustice to be at all involuntary. There is also in jealousy, as they suppose, something involuntary; and for this reason they confess to jealousy also.
discourses_of-inconsistency.plainEnglish: The main problem is that people are confused and inconsistent about what's good and what's bad. Different people have different reasons for this. Usually, they won't admit to what they think is shameful. They think being timid shows good character. They think being overly sympathetic is also good. But they think being foolish is what slaves do. They won't admit to things that hurt society. But they will confess to most other mistakes. Why? Because they think these mistakes are involuntary — like timidity and too much sympathy. If someone admits they lack self-control, they blame it on passion. They say it's not their fault. But people don't think injustice is involuntary. They also think jealousy just happens to them involuntarily. So they'll confess to being jealous too.

discourses_of-inconsistency.originalText: Living then among such men, who are so confused, so ignorant of what they say, and of the evils which they have or have not, and why they have them, or how they shall be relieved of them, I think it is worth the trouble for a man to watch constantly (and to ask) whether I also am one of them, what imagination I have about myself, how I conduct myself, whether I conduct myself as a prudent man, whether I conduct myself as a temperate man, whether I ever say this, that I have been taught to be prepared for everything that may happen. Have I the consciousness, which a man who knows nothing ought to have, that I know nothing? Do I go to my teacher as men go to oracles, prepared to obey? or do I like a snivelling boy go to my school to learn history and understand the books which I did not understand before, and, if it should happen so, to explain them also to others?
discourses_of-inconsistency.plainEnglish: You live surrounded by people who are completely confused. They don't know what they're saying. They don't understand what problems they have or don't have, why they have them, or how to fix them. Given this situation, I think it's worth the effort to constantly watch yourself and ask: Am I one of them too? What do I imagine about myself? How do I actually behave? Do I act like a wise person? Do I act with self-control? Do I ever claim that I've been taught to handle whatever happens? Do I have the humility that someone who knows nothing should have — the awareness that I know nothing? When I go to my teacher, do I go like people go to oracles, ready to obey? Or do I go like some whining schoolboy just trying to learn facts and understand books I didn't get before, so I can maybe explain them to others later?

discourses_of-inconsistency.originalText: Man, you have had a fight in the house with a poor slave, you have turned the family upside down, you have frightened the neighbors, and you come to me as if you were a wise man, and you take your seat and judge how I have explained some word, and how I have babbled whatever came into my head. You come full of envy, and humbled, because you bring nothing from home; and you sit during the discussion thinking of nothing else than how your father is disposed towards you and your brother. What are they saying about me there? now they think that I am improving, and are saying, He will return with all knowledge. I wish I could learn everything before I return; but much labor is necessary, and no one sends me anything, and the baths at Nicopolis are dirty; everything is bad at home, and bad here.
discourses_of-inconsistency.plainEnglish: You got into a fight at home with some poor slave. You turned your whole household upside down. You scared the neighbors. Then you come to me acting like you're some wise person. You sit down and judge how I explained some word or how I rambled about whatever popped into my head. You show up full of jealousy and feeling small because you're bringing nothing from home. During our discussions, you're not thinking about anything except how your father feels about you and your brother. 'What are they saying about me back there? They probably think I'm getting better and saying, He'll come back knowing everything.' I wish I could learn it all before I go home. But it takes hard work. Nobody sends me anything. The baths here in Nicopolis are filthy. Everything's bad at home, and everything's bad here.

discourses_on-friendship.originalText: What a man applies himself to earnestly, that he naturally loves. Do men then apply themselves earnestly to the things which are bad? By no means. Well, do they apply themselves to things which in no way concern themselves? Not to these either. It remains then that they employ themselves earnestly only about things which are good; and if they are earnestly employed about things, they love such things also. Whoever then understands what is good can also know how to love; but he who cannot distinguish good from bad, and things which are neither good nor bad from both, how can he possess the power of loving? To love, then, is only in the power of the wise.
discourses_on-friendship.plainEnglish: Whatever you put serious effort into, you naturally love. Do people put serious effort into bad things? No way. Do they put effort into things that don't matter to them at all? No, not those either. So people only put real effort into good things. And if they're putting effort into something, they love it too. Anyone who truly understands what's good can also know how to love. But someone who can't tell good from bad, or figure out what's neither good nor bad — how could they know how to love? Only wise people can truly love.

discourses_on-friendship.originalText: For universally, be not deceived, every animal is attached to nothing so much as to its own interests. Whatever then appears to it an impediment to this interest, whether this be a brother, or a father, or a child, or beloved, or lover, it hates, spurns, curses; for its nature is to love nothing so much as its own interests: this is father, and brother, and kinsman, and country, and God. When then the gods appear to us to be an impediment to this, we abuse them and throw down their statues and burn their temples, as Alexander ordered the temples of Aesculapius to be burned when his dear friend died.
discourses_on-friendship.plainEnglish: Don't fool yourself — every creature cares about nothing more than its own interests. Whatever seems to block those interests, it will hate. Doesn't matter if it's a brother, father, child, beloved, or lover. The creature will reject them, push them away, curse them. This is just nature — nothing matters more than self-interest. Self-interest is father, brother, family, country, and God all rolled into one. So when the gods seem to block what we want, we curse them. We tear down their statues. We burn their temples. Just like Alexander ordered the temples of Aesculapius burned when his dear friend died.

discourses_on-friendship.originalText: For this reason, if a man put in the same place his interest, sanctity, goodness, and country, and parents, and friends, all these are secured: but if he puts in one place his interest, in another his friends, and his country and his kinsmen and justice itself, all these give way, being borne down by the weight of interest. For where the I and the Mine are placed, to that place of necessity the animal inclines; if in the flesh, there is the ruling power; if in the will, it is there; and if it is in externals, it is there. If then I am there where my will is, then only shall I be a friend such as I ought to be, and son, and father; for this will be my interest, to maintain the character of fidelity, of modesty, of patience, of abstinence, of active co-operation, of observing my relations (towards all). But if I put myself in one place, and honesty in another, then the doctrine of Epicurus becomes strong, which asserts either that there is no honesty or it is that which opinion holds to be honest (virtuous).
discourses_on-friendship.plainEnglish: Here's the key: if you put your true interest in the same place as your integrity, goodness, country, parents, and friends, then all of these are safe. But if you put your interest in one place and your friends, country, family, and justice in another place, then all of these will be trampled. They get crushed under the weight of your selfish interest. Whatever you care about most — that's where you'll naturally go. If you care most about physical pleasure, that rules you. If you care most about your choices and character, that rules you. If you care most about external things, that rules you. Only when I am where my will is — only then will I be the kind of friend I should be, and son, and father. Because then it will be in my interest to stay faithful, modest, patient, self-controlled, and helpful. It will be in my interest to honor my relationships. But if I put myself in one place and honesty in another, then Epicurus wins. His teaching says that either virtue doesn't exist, or virtue is just whatever people think is virtuous.

discourses_on-friendship.originalText: It was through this ignorance that the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians quarrelled, and the Thebans with both; and the great king quarrelled with Hellas, and the Macedonians with both: and the Romans with the Getae. And still earlier the Trojan war happened for these reasons. Alexander was the guest of Menelaus, and if any man had seen their friendly disposition, he would not have believed any one who said that they were not friends. But there was cast between them (as between dogs) a bit of meat, a handsome woman, and about her war arose.
discourses_on-friendship.plainEnglish: This ignorance is what caused the Athenians and Spartans to fight each other. The Thebans fought both of them. The Persian king fought the Greeks, and the Macedonians fought both sides. The Romans fought the Getae. Even earlier, the Trojan War happened for the same reasons. Alexander was Menelaus's guest. If you had seen how friendly they were, you wouldn't have believed anyone who said they weren't friends. But something was thrown between them — like a piece of meat thrown between dogs. In this case, it was a beautiful woman. And that's what started the war.

discourses_on-friendship.originalText: And now when you see brothers to be friends appearing to have one mind, do not conclude from this anything about their friendship, not even if they swear it and say that it is impossible for them to be separated from one another. For the ruling principle of a bad man cannot be trusted; it is insecure, has no certain rule by which it is directed, and is overpowered at different times by different appearances. But examine, not what other men examine, if they are born of the same parents and brought up together, and under the same pedagogue; but examine this only, wherein they place their interest, whether in externals or in the will. If in externals, do not name them friends, no more than name them trustworthy or constant, or brave or free; do not name them even men, if you have any judgment.
discourses_on-friendship.plainEnglish: When you see brothers who seem friendly and claim they think alike, don't assume anything about their friendship. Don't believe them even if they swear they could never be separated. You can't trust the mind of a bad person. It's unstable. It has no solid principles to guide it. Different situations will push it in different directions. Don't look at what most people look at — whether they have the same parents, grew up together, or had the same teacher. Look at this instead: what do they really care about? Do they care about external things or about their own choices? If they care about externals, don't call them friends. Don't call them trustworthy, steady, brave, or free either. If you have any sense, don't even call them real human beings.

discourses_on-friendship.originalText: For that is not a principle of human nature which makes them bite one another, and abuse one another, and occupy deserted places or public places, as if they were mountains, and in the courts of justice display the acts of robbers; nor yet that which makes them intemperate and adulterers and corrupters, nor that which makes them do whatever else men do against one another through this one opinion only, that of placing themselves and their interests in the things which are not within the power of their will. But if you hear that in truth these men think the good to be only there, where will is, and where there is a right use of appearances, no longer trouble yourself whether they are father or son, or brothers, or have associated a long time and are companions, but when you have ascertained this only, confidently declare that they are friends, as you declare that they are faithful, that they are just. For where else is friendship than where there is fidelity, and modesty, where there is a communion of honest things and of nothing else.
discourses_on-friendship.plainEnglish:
What makes people bite each other, abuse each other, and fight over empty places or public spaces like wild animals? What makes them act like robbers in courtrooms? What makes them lustful, unfaithful, and corrupt? What makes them do all the terrible things they do to each other? It's one simple mistake: they put themselves and their interests in things they can't actually control.

But when you hear that people truly believe good things only exist where their will is — where they use their judgments correctly — then don't worry about whether they're your father, son, brothers, or old friends. Once you know this about them, you can confidently call them friends. You can say they're trustworthy and just. Where else can friendship exist except where there's loyalty, decency, and a shared commitment to honest things — and nothing else?

discourses_on-friendship.originalText: But you may say, Such a one treated me with regard so long; and did he not love me? How do you know, slave, if he did not regard you in the same way as he wipes his shoes with a sponge, or as he takes care of his beast? How do you know, when you have ceased to be useful as a vessel, he will not throw you away like a broken platter? But this woman is my wife, and we have lived together so long. And how long did Eriphyle live with Amphiaraus, and was the mother of children and of many? But a necklace came between them: and what is a necklace? It is the opinion about such things. That was the bestial principle, that was the thing which broke asunder the friendship between husband and wife, that which did not allow the woman to be a wife nor the mother to be a mother.
discourses_on-friendship.plainEnglish: But you might say, "This person treated me well for so long. Didn't he love me?" How do you know, fool, that he didn't regard you the same way he uses a sponge to wipe his shoes? Or the way he takes care of his livestock? How do you know that once you're no longer useful to him, he won't throw you away like a broken dish? "But this woman is my wife. We've lived together for years." So what? How long did Eriphyle live with Amphiaraus? She was the mother of his children — many of them. But a necklace came between them. And what is a necklace? It's just your opinion about such things. That was the animal instinct in her. That's what destroyed the friendship between husband and wife. That's what stopped the woman from being a wife and the mother from being a mother.

discourses_on-friendship.originalText: And let every man among you who has seriously resolved either to be a friend himself or to have another for his friend, cut out these opinions, hate them, drive them from his soul. And thus first of all he will not reproach himself, he will not be at variance with himself, he will not change his mind, he will not torture himself. In the next place, to another also, who is like himself, he will be altogether and completely a friend. But he will bear with the man who is unlike himself, he will be kind to him, gentle, ready to pardon on account of his ignorance, on account of his being mistaken in things of the greatest importance; but he will be harsh to no man, being well convinced of Plato's doctrine that every mind is deprived of truth unwillingly. If you cannot do this, yet you can do in all other respects as friends do, drink together, and lodge together, and sail together, and you may be born of the same parents, for snakes also are: but neither will they be friends, nor you, so long as you retain these bestial and cursed opinions.
discourses_on-friendship.plainEnglish: If you want to be a true friend or have true friends, you need to cut out certain toxic opinions. Hate them. Drive them from your soul. When you do this, you'll stop beating yourself up. You won't fight with yourself or keep changing your mind. You won't torture yourself. And with other people who think like you, you'll be a complete friend. With people who don't think like you, you'll still be patient. You'll be kind and gentle. You'll forgive them because they don't know better — they're just wrong about important things. But you won't be harsh with anyone. Remember what Plato taught: every mind loses truth against its will. If you can't manage this, you can still do what friends normally do. You can drink together, live together, travel together. You might even be born from the same parents. Snakes are born from the same parents too. But neither snakes nor you will be real friends as long as you hold onto these brutal, poisonous opinions.

discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.originalText:
Every man will read a book with more pleasure or even with more ease, if it is written in fairer characters. Therefore every man will also listen more readily to what is spoken, if it is signified by appropriate and becoming words. We must not say then that there is no faculty of expression: for this affirmation is the characteristic of an impious and also of a timid man. Of an impious man, because he undervalues the gifts which come from God, just as if he would take away the commodity of the power of vision, or hearing, or of seeing. Has then God given you eyes to no purpose? and to no purpose has he infused into them a spirit so strong and of such skilful contrivance as to reach a long way and to fashion the forms of things which are seen? What messenger is so swift and vigilant? And to no purpose has he made the interjacent atmosphere so efficacious and elastic that the vision penetrates through the atmosphere which is in a manner moved? And to no purpose has he made light, without the presence of which there would be no use in any other thing?

Man, be neither ungrateful for these gifts nor yet forget the things which are superior to them. But indeed for the power of seeing and hearing, and indeed for life itself, and for the things which contribute to support it, for the fruits which are dry, and for wine and oil give thanks to God: but remember that he has given you something else better than all these, I mean the power of using them, proving them, and estimating the value of each.
discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.plainEnglish: Everyone enjoys reading a book more when it's written in clear, beautiful handwriting. In the same way, people listen more carefully when you use the right words that fit what you're saying. So don't claim that speaking well doesn't matter. That's what godless and cowardly people say. Godless because they dismiss the gifts God gave us — like claiming vision or hearing are worthless. Did God give you eyes for no reason? Did he waste his time putting such powerful and skillful energy into them that they can see far distances and make sense of what they see? What messenger moves as fast and stays as alert as your vision? Did he pointlessly make the air so effective and flexible that your sight can pass right through it? Did he create light for no reason, when without it nothing else would work? Don't be ungrateful for these gifts, but don't forget about the even greater things either. Yes, be thankful to God for your ability to see and hear, for life itself, and for everything that keeps you alive — dried fruits, wine, and oil. But remember: he gave you something better than all of these. He gave you the power to use them, test them, and figure out what each one is worth.

discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.originalText: For what is that which gives information about each of these powers, what each of them is worth? Is it each faculty itself? Did you ever hear the faculty of vision saying anything about itself? or the faculty of hearing? or wheat, or barley, or a horse, or a dog? No; but they are appointed as ministers and slaves to serve the faculty which has the power of making use of the appearances of things. And if you inquire what is the value of each thing, of whom do you inquire? who answers you? How then can any other faculty be more powerful than this, which uses the rest as ministers and itself proves each and pronounces about them? for which of them knows what itself is, and what is its own value? which of them knows when it ought to employ itself and when not? what faculty is it which opens and closes the eyes, and turns them away from objects to which it ought not to apply them and does apply them to other objects? Is it the faculty of vision? No, but it is the faculty of the will.
discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.plainEnglish: What is it that judges each of these abilities? What tells you what each one is worth? Does each ability judge itself? Have you ever heard your eyesight comment on itself? Or your hearing? Or wheat, barley, a horse, or a dog? No. They're all servants. They serve the one ability that can use what your senses show you. And when you ask what something is worth, who do you ask? Who gives you the answer? So how could any other ability be more powerful than this one? This one uses all the others as servants. It tests them and makes judgments about them. Which of your other abilities knows what it is or what it's worth? Which one knows when to work and when to stop? What makes your eyes open and close? What turns them away from things they shouldn't look at and toward things they should? Is it your eyesight? No. It's your will.

discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.originalText: What is that faculty which closes and opens the ears? what is that by which they are curious and inquisitive, or on the contrary unmoved by what is said? is it the faculty of hearing? It is no other than the faculty of the will. Will this faculty then, seeing that it is amidst all the other faculties which are blind and dumb and unable to see anything else except the very acts for which they are appointed in order to minister to this (faculty) and serve it, but this faculty alone sees sharp and sees what is the value of each of the rest; will this faculty declare to us that anything else is the best, or that itself is? And what else does the eye do when it is opened than see? But whether we ought to look on the wife of a certain person, and in what manner, who tells us? The faculty of the will. And whether we ought to believe what is said or not to believe it, and if we do believe, whether we ought to be moved by it or not, who tells us? Is it not the faculty of the will?
discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.plainEnglish: What controls whether you listen or tune out? What makes you curious about some things but leaves you cold toward others? Is it just your ears? No. It's your will. Your will sits among all your other abilities — which are blind and deaf and can only do their basic jobs to serve your will. But your will alone sees clearly. It judges what each ability is worth. So will your will tell you that something else is most important? Or that it itself is? What does your eye do except see when you open it? But who decides whether you should look at someone's wife, and how you should look? Your will decides. Who decides whether to believe what you hear, and whether to let it affect you? Your will.

discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.originalText: But if you ask me what then is the most excellent of all things, what must I say? I cannot say the power of speaking, but the power of the will, when it is right ([Greek: orthae]). For it is this which uses the other (the power of speaking), and all the other faculties both small and great. For when this faculty of the will is set right, a man who is not good becomes good: but when it fails, a man becomes bad. It is through this that we are unfortunate, that we are fortunate, that we blame one another, are pleased with one another. In a word, it is this which if we neglect it makes unhappiness, and if we carefully look after it, makes happiness.
discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.plainEnglish: But if you ask me what the most excellent thing is, what should I say? I can't say it's the power of speaking. It's the power of the will, when it's set right. This is what controls your speaking power and all your other abilities, big and small. When your will is set right, a bad person becomes good. When it fails, a person becomes bad. This is why we're unlucky or lucky. This is why we blame each other or are pleased with each other. In short, if we ignore our will, we become unhappy. If we take careful care of it, we become happy.

discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.originalText: What then is usually done? Men generally act as a traveller would do on his way to his own country, when he enters a good inn, and being pleased with it should remain there. Man, you have forgotten your purpose: you were not travelling to this inn, but you were passing through it. But this is a pleasant inn. And how many other inns are pleasant? and how many meadows are pleasant? yet only for passing through. But your purpose is this, to return to your country, to relieve your kinsmen of anxiety, to discharge the duties of a citizen, to marry, to beget children, to fill the usual magistracies. For you are not come to select more pleasant places, but to live in these where you were born and of which you were made a citizen. Something of the kind takes place in the matter which we are considering. Since by the aid of speech and such communication as you receive here you must advance to perfection, and purge your will and correct the faculty which makes use of the appearances of things; and since it is necessary also for the teaching (delivery) of theorems to be effected by a certain mode of expression and with a certain variety and sharpness, some persons captivated by these very things abide in them, one captivated by the expression, another by syllogisms, another again by sophisms, and still another by some other inn ([Greek: paudocheiou]) of the kind; and there they stay and waste away as they were among sirens.
discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.plainEnglish:
What usually happens? People act like travelers who find a nice inn on the way home. They like it so much they decide to stay there. But you've forgotten your purpose — you weren't traveling to the inn. You were just passing through it. "But this is such a pleasant inn!" Sure. And how many other inns are pleasant? How many meadows are beautiful? They're all just for passing through. Your real purpose is to get home, to ease your family's worries, to do your civic duties, to marry, have children, and serve in public office. You didn't come here to pick out the most pleasant spots. You came to live where you were born and where you're a citizen.

The same thing happens with philosophy. You use speech and the lessons you get here to move toward perfection. You purge your will and fix the part of your mind that deals with how things appear to you. Teaching requires a certain way of speaking — with variety and sharpness. But some people get captivated by these very tools. One person falls in love with elegant expression. Another gets obsessed with logical arguments. Another with clever tricks of reasoning. Another with some other roadside attraction. They stay there and waste away, like sailors trapped by sirens.

discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.originalText:
Man, your purpose (business) was to make yourself capable of using conformably to nature the appearances presented to you, in your desires not to be frustrated, in your aversion from things not to fall into that which you would avoid, never to have no luck (as one may say), nor ever to have bad luck, to be free, not hindered, not compelled, conforming yourself to the administration of Zeus, obeying it, well satisfied with this, blaming no one, charging no one with fault, able from your whole soul to utter these verses:

Lead me, O Zeus, and thou too Destiny.
discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.plainEnglish: Your job was to learn how to handle life's events naturally. To get what you want without being crushed when you don't get it. To avoid what you dislike without falling into what you're trying to escape. To never feel unlucky or cursed. To be free — not blocked, not forced, not pushed around. To accept how Zeus runs the world. To obey willingly and be satisfied with it. To blame no one. To accuse no one of wrongdoing. To say from your heart: Lead me, Zeus, and you too, Destiny.

discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.originalText: TO (OR AGAINST) A PERSON WHO WAS ONE OF THOSE WHO WERE NOT VALUED (ESTEEMED) BY HIM.—A certain person said to him (Epictetus): Frequently I desired to hear you and came to you, and you never gave me any answer; and now, if it is possible, I entreat you to say something to me. Do you think, said Epictetus, that as there is an art in anything else, so there is also an art in speaking, and that he who has the art, will speak skilfully, and he who has not, will speak unskilfully?—I do think so.—He then who by speaking receives benefit himself, and is able to benefit others, will speak skilfully; but he who is rather damaged by speaking and does damage to others, will he be unskilled in this art of speaking? And you may find that some are damaged and others benefited by speaking. And are all who hear benefited by what they hear? Or will you find that among them also some are benefited and some damaged? There are both among these also, he said.
discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.plainEnglish: Someone once said to Epictetus: "I've often wanted to hear you speak and come to visit you, but you never answered me. Please, if you can, say something to me now." Epictetus replied: "Do you think there's skill involved in speaking, just like there's skill in everything else? The person with skill speaks well, and the person without skill speaks poorly?" "Yes, I think so," the person said. "So the person who benefits himself and helps others when he speaks — he's skilled at speaking. But the person who harms himself and others when he speaks — he lacks this skill, right? You'll find that some people are hurt by speaking and others are helped by it. And are all listeners helped by what they hear? Or do you find that some listeners benefit and some are harmed?" "Both," the person said.

discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.originalText: In this case also then those who hear skilfully are benefited, and those who hear unskilfully are damaged? He admitted this. Is there then a skill in hearing also, as there is in speaking? It seems so. If you choose, consider the matter in this way also. The practice of music, to whom does it belong? To a musician. And the proper making of a statue, to whom do you think that it belongs? To a statuary. And the looking at a statue skilfully, does this appear to you to require the aid of no art? This also requires the aid of art. Then if speaking properly is the business of the skilful man, do you see that to hear also with benefit is the business of the skilful man? Now as to speaking and hearing perfectly, and usefully, let us for the present, if you please, say no more, for both of us are a long way from everything of the kind. But I think that every man will allow this, that he who is going to hear philosophers requires some amount of practice in hearing. Is it not so?
discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.plainEnglish: So the people who listen well benefit, and the people who listen poorly get hurt? He agreed. Is there a skill to listening, just like there's a skill to speaking? It seems like it. If you want, think about it this way. Music — who does that belong to? A musician. Making a statue properly — who do you think that belongs to? A sculptor. And looking at a statue skillfully — does that seem like it needs no art? That needs art too. So if speaking well is the job of a skilled person, do you see that listening with benefit is also the job of a skilled person? Now, about speaking and listening perfectly and usefully — let's drop that topic for now, if you don't mind. Both of us are nowhere near that level. But I think everyone will agree on this: anyone who's going to listen to philosophers needs some practice in listening. Don't you think so?

discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.originalText: Why then do you say nothing to me? I can only say this to you, that he who knows not who he is, and for what purpose he exists, and what is this world, and with whom he is associated, and what things are the good and the bad, and the beautiful and the ugly, and who neither understands discourse nor demonstration, nor what is true nor what is false, and who is not able to distinguish them, will neither desire according to nature nor turn away nor move towards, nor intend (to act), nor assent, nor dissent, nor suspend his judgment: to say all in a few words, he will go about dumb and blind, thinking that he is somebody, but being nobody. Is this so now for the first time? Is it not the fact that ever since the human race existed, all errors and misfortunes have arisen through this ignorance?
discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.plainEnglish: Why don't you say anything to me? Here's what I can tell you: If you don't know who you are, why you exist, what this world is, who you're connected to, what's good and bad, beautiful and ugly — if you can't understand reasoning or proof, can't tell truth from lies — then you won't want the right things or avoid the right things. You won't move toward what's good or make plans or agree or disagree or hold back judgment properly. To put it simply: you'll stumble through life deaf and blind, thinking you're somebody important when you're really nobody. Is this happening for the first time? Haven't all human mistakes and disasters come from exactly this kind of ignorance since people first existed?

discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.originalText: This is all that I have to say to you; and I say even this not willingly. Why? Because you have not roused me. For what must I look to in order to be roused, as men who are expert in riding are roused by generous horses? Must I look to your body? You treat it disgracefully. To your dress? That is luxurious. To your behavior, to your look? That is the same as nothing. When you would listen to a philosopher, do not say to him, You tell me nothing; but only show yourself worthy of hearing or fit for hearing; and you will see how you will move the speaker.
discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.plainEnglish: This is all I have to say to you. And honestly, I don't even want to say this much. Why? Because you haven't inspired me to teach you. What should get me excited about teaching you, the way skilled riders get excited by good horses? Should I look at your body? You neglect it. Your clothes? They're fancy and soft. Your behavior and appearance? They're worthless. When you want to listen to a philosopher, don't tell him "You're not teaching me anything." Instead, show that you're worthy of hearing something — show that you're ready to learn. Then you'll see how you can motivate a teacher to really speak.

discourses_that-logic-is-necessary.originalText:
When one of those who were present said,
Persuade me that logic is necessary, he replied, Do you wish me to
prove this to you? The answer was, Yes. Then I must use a demonstrative
form of speech. This was granted. How then will you know if I am
cheating you by my argument? The man was silent. Do you see, said
Epictetus, that you yourself are admitting that logic is necessary, if
without it you cannot know so much as this, whether logic is necessary
or not necessary?
discourses_that-logic-is-necessary.plainEnglish: Someone at the lecture said, "Convince me that logic is necessary." Epictetus replied, "Do you want me to prove it to you?" The man said yes. "Then I'll have to use logical arguments," Epictetus said. The man agreed. "But how will you know if I'm tricking you with my reasoning?" The man had no answer. "See?" said Epictetus. "You just admitted that logic is necessary. Without it, you can't even figure out whether logic itself is necessary or not."

discourses_of-finery-in-dress.originalText: A certain young man, a rhetorician, came to see Epictetus, with his hair dressed more carefully than was usual and his attire in an ornamental style; whereupon Epictetus said, Tell me if you do not think that some dogs are beautiful and some horses, and so of all other animals. I do think so, the youth replied. Are not then some men also beautiful and others ugly? Certainly. Do we then for the same reason call each of them in the same kind beautiful, or each beautiful for something peculiar? And you will judge of this matter thus. Since we see a dog naturally formed for one thing, and a horse for another, and for another still, as an example, a nightingale, we may generally and not improperly declare each of them to be beautiful then when it is most excellent according to its nature; but since the nature of each is different, each of them seems to me to be beautiful in a different way. Is it not so? He admitted that it was.
discourses_of-finery-in-dress.plainEnglish: A young man who taught rhetoric came to visit Epictetus. His hair was styled more carefully than usual and his clothes were fancy. Epictetus said to him, "Tell me — don't you think some dogs are beautiful and some horses are beautiful? And the same with all other animals?" "Yes, I do," the young man replied. "Well then, aren't some people beautiful and others ugly?" "Certainly." "Do we call them beautiful for the same reasons, or does each one have something unique that makes it beautiful? Think about it this way. We see that a dog is naturally made for one purpose, a horse for another, and a nightingale for yet another. So we can rightly say each one is beautiful when it's most excellent according to its own nature. But since each has a different nature, each one is beautiful in a different way. Isn't that right?" The young man agreed.

discourses_of-finery-in-dress.originalText: That then which makes a dog beautiful, makes a horse ugly; and that which makes a horse beautiful, makes a dog ugly, if it is true that their natures are different. It seems to be so. For I think that what makes a Pancratiast beautiful, makes a wrestler to be not good, and a runner to be most ridiculous; and he who is beautiful for the Pentathlon, is very ugly for wrestling. It is so, said he. What then makes a man beautiful? Is it that which in its kind makes both a dog and a horse beautiful? It is, he said. What then makes a dog beautiful? The possession of the excellence of a dog. And what makes a horse beautiful? The possession of the excellence of a horse. What then makes a man beautiful? Is it not the possession of the excellence of a man?
discourses_of-finery-in-dress.plainEnglish: What makes a dog beautiful makes a horse ugly. What makes a horse beautiful makes a dog ugly. This is true because they have different natures. Think about it this way: what makes someone good at one sport often makes them bad at another. A boxer's build might make him terrible at running. Someone perfect for one competition looks completely wrong for wrestling. So what makes a human beautiful? The same principle that makes both dogs and horses beautiful in their own way. What makes a dog beautiful? Having the excellence that belongs to dogs. What makes a horse beautiful? Having the excellence that belongs to horses. So what makes a human beautiful? Having the excellence that belongs to humans.

discourses_of-finery-in-dress.originalText: And do you then, if you wish to be beautiful, young man, labor at this, the acquisition of human excellence? But what is this? Observe whom you yourself praise, when you praise many persons without partiality: do you praise the just or the unjust? The just. Whether do you praise the moderate or the immoderate? The moderate. And the temperate or the intemperate? The temperate. If then you make yourself such a person, you will know that you will make yourself beautiful; but so long as you neglect these things, you must be ugly ([Greek: aischron]), even though you contrive all you can to appear beautiful.
discourses_of-finery-in-dress.plainEnglish: So if you want to be beautiful, young man, work on this: becoming an excellent human being. But what does that mean? Look at who you praise when you're being honest. Do you praise fair people or unfair people? Fair people. Do you praise people with self-control or people without it? People with self-control. Do you praise people who are disciplined or undisciplined? Disciplined people. If you make yourself that kind of person, you'll know you've made yourself beautiful. But as long as you ignore these things, you'll be ugly — no matter how hard you try to look good on the outside.

discourses_in-what-a-man-ought-to-be-exe.originalText: There are three things (topics, [Greek: topoi]) in which a man ought to exercise himself who would be wise and good. The first concerns the desires and the aversions, that a man may not fail to get what he desires, and that he may not fall into that which he does not desire. The second concerns the movements towards an object and the movements from an object, and generally in doing what a man ought to do, that he may act according to order, to reason, and not carelessly. The third thing concerns freedom from deception and rashness in judgment, and generally it concerns the assents ([Greek: sugchatatheseis]). Of these topics the chief and the most urgent is that which relates to the affects ([Greek: ta pathae] perturbations); for an affect is produced in no other way than by a failing to obtain that which a man desires or falling into that which a man would wish to avoid. This is that which brings in perturbations, disorders, bad fortune, misfortunes, sorrows, lamentations, and envy; that which makes men envious and jealous; and by these causes we are unable even to listen to the precepts of reason. The second topic concerns the duties of a man; for I ought not to be free from affects ([Greek: apathae]) like a statue, but I ought to maintain the relations ([Greek: scheseis]) natural and acquired, as a pious man, as a son, as a father, as a citizen.
discourses_in-what-a-man-ought-to-be-exe.plainEnglish: There are three areas you need to work on if you want to be wise and good. First, manage your desires and what you want to avoid. Don't fail to get what you truly want, and don't end up with what you don't want. Second, handle your actions properly. Move toward things and away from things the right way. Do what you should do with order and reason, not carelessly. Third, avoid being fooled and making rash judgments. Be careful about what you agree with and accept as true. The first area is the most important and urgent. It deals with your emotions. You get upset only when you fail to get what you want or when you get what you're trying to avoid. This is what causes all your troubles — disorder, bad luck, misfortune, sadness, complaints, and envy. It makes you envious and jealous. When you're caught up in these feelings, you can't even listen to reason. The second area deals with your duties. You shouldn't be emotionless like a statue. You need to maintain your natural and learned relationships. Be a good person, a good son, a good father, a good citizen.

discourses_in-what-a-man-ought-to-be-exe.originalText: The third topic is that which immediately concerns those who are making proficiency, that which concerns the security of the other two, so that not even in sleep any appearance unexamined may surprise us, nor in intoxication, nor in melancholy. This, it may be said, is above our power. But the present philosophers neglecting the first topic and the second (the affects and duties), employ themselves on the third, using sophistical arguments ([Greek: metapiptontas]), making conclusions from questioning, employing hypotheses, lying. For a man must, it is said, when employed on these matters, take care that he is not deceived. Who must? The wise and good man. This then is all that is wanting to you. Have you successfully worked out the rest? Are you free from deception in the matter of money? If you see a beautiful girl do you resist the appearance? If your neighbor obtains an estate by will, are you not vexed? Now is there nothing else wanting to you except unchangeable firmness of mind ([Greek: ametaptosia])?
discourses_in-what-a-man-ought-to-be-exe.plainEnglish: The third area of training deals with securing the first two areas. It's about making sure no untested thought catches you off guard — not when you're asleep, drunk, or depressed. People say this is beyond our power. But today's philosophers skip the first two areas (emotions and duties) and jump straight to the third. They use clever tricks, draw conclusions from questions, and work with hypotheticals. They're basically lying. They say a person working on these matters must be careful not to get deceived. Who must? The wise and good person. So that's all you need, right? Have you mastered everything else? Are you free from deception about money? When you see a beautiful woman, do you resist the urge? When your neighbor inherits wealth, are you not bothered? Is the only thing you lack an unshakeable mind?

discourses_in-what-a-man-ought-to-be-exe.originalText: Wretch, you hear these very things with fear and anxiety that some person may despise you, and with inquiries about what any person may say about you. And if a man come and tell you that in a certain conversation in which the question was, Who is the best philosopher, a man who was present said that a certain person was the chief philosopher, your little soul which was only a finger's length stretches out to two cubits. But if another who is present says, You are mistaken; it is not worth while to listen to a certain person, for what does he know? he has only the first principles, and no more? then you are confounded, you grow pale, you cry out immediately, I will show him who I am, that I am a great philosopher. It is seen by these very things: why do you wish to show it by others? Do you not know that Diogenes pointed out one of the sophists in this way by stretching out his middle finger? And then when the man was wild with rage, This, he said, is the certain person: I have pointed him out to you. For a man is not shown by the finger, as a stone or a piece of wood; but when any person shows the man's principles, then he shows him as a man.
discourses_in-what-a-man-ought-to-be-exe.plainEnglish: You pathetic fool, you listen to these teachings with fear and worry that someone might look down on you. You fret about what people say about you. If someone comes and tells you that in some conversation about who the best philosopher is, someone said a certain person was the greatest philosopher, your tiny soul — which was only finger-sized — suddenly swells up to enormous proportions. But if someone else who was there says, "You're wrong. That person isn't worth listening to. What does he really know? He only has the basics, nothing more," then you're thrown into chaos. You turn pale. You immediately cry out, "I'll show him who I am! I'm a great philosopher!" These very reactions reveal the truth about you. Why do you want to prove it through other means? Don't you know how Diogenes exposed one of the sophists? He just held up his middle finger at him. When the man flew into a rage, Diogenes said, "There — that's the person you're asking about. I've pointed him out to you." You can't show what a person is by pointing at them like you would a rock or piece of wood. When you reveal someone's principles, then you show them as they really are.

discourses_in-what-a-man-ought-to-be-exe.originalText: Let us look at your principles also. For is it not plain that you value not at all your own will ([Greek: proairesis]), but you look externally to things which are independent of your will? For instance, what will a certain person say? and what will people think of you? Will you be considered a man of learning; have you read Chrysippus or Antipater? for if you have read Archedamus also, you have every thing (that you can desire). Why you are still uneasy lest you should not show us who you are? Would you let me tell you what manner of man you have shown us that you are? You have exhibited yourself to us as a mean fellow, querulous, passionate, cowardly, finding fault with everything, blaming everybody, never quiet, vain: this is what you have exhibited to us. Go away now and read Archedamus; then if a mouse should leap down and make a noise, you are a dead man. For such a death awaits you as it did—what was the man's name—Crinis; and he too was proud, because he understood Archedamus.
discourses_in-what-a-man-ought-to-be-exe.plainEnglish: Let's look at your principles too. Isn't it obvious that you don't care about your own choices at all? Instead, you focus on things outside your control. Like: what will someone say about you? What will people think? Will they see you as educated? Have you read Chrysippus or Antipater? If you've also read Archedamus, then you think you have everything you need. Why are you still worried that you haven't shown us who you really are? Want me to tell you what kind of person you've actually shown us? You've shown yourself to be petty, whiny, angry, cowardly — always complaining about everything, blaming everyone, never at peace, totally vain. That's what you've shown us. Go read Archedamus now. Then when a mouse jumps down and makes a noise, you'll be scared to death. That's the kind of death waiting for you — just like what's-his-name, Crinis. He was proud too because he understood Archedamus.

discourses_in-what-a-man-ought-to-be-exe.originalText: Wretch, will you not dismiss these things that do not concern you at all? These things are suitable to those who are able to learn them without perturbation, to those who can say: "I am not subject to anger, to grief, to envy: I am not hindered, I am not restrained. What remains for me? I have leisure, I am tranquil: let us see how we must deal with sophistical arguments; let us see how when a man has accepted an hypothesis he shall not be led away to any thing absurd." To them such things belong. To those who are happy it is appropriate to light a fire, to dine; if they choose, both to sing and to dance. But when the vessel is sinking, you come to me and hoist the sails.
discourses_in-what-a-man-ought-to-be-exe.plainEnglish: You fool, stop worrying about things that don't matter to you at all! These academic exercises are for people who can learn them without getting worked up. They're for people who can say: "I don't get angry, sad, or jealous. Nothing blocks me or holds me back. What's left for me to do? I have free time and I'm calm. Let me figure out how to handle tricky arguments. Let me see how someone can accept a premise without being led to something ridiculous." That stuff is for them. When people are happy, it makes sense for them to light a fire and eat dinner. If they want, they can sing and dance too. But when the ship is sinking, you come to me asking to put up the sails.

discourses_what-is-the-matter-on-which-a.originalText: The material for the wise and good man is his own ruling faculty: and the body is the material for the physician and the aliptes (the man who oils persons); the land is the matter for the husbandman. The business of the wise and good man is to use appearances conformably to nature: and as it is the nature of every soul to assent to the truth, to dissent from the false, and to remain in suspense as to that which is uncertain; so it is its nature to be moved towards the desire for the good, and to aversion from the evil; and with respect to that which is neither good nor bad it feels indifferent. For as the money-changer (banker) is not allowed to reject Cæsar's coin, nor the seller of herbs, but if you show the coin, whether he chooses or not, he must give up what is sold for the coin; so it is also in the matter of the soul. When the good appears, it immediately attracts to itself; the evil repels from itself. But the soul will never reject the manifest appearance of the good, any more than persons will reject Cæsar's coin. On this principle depends every movement both of man and God.
discourses_what-is-the-matter-on-which-a.plainEnglish: The wise person's raw material is their own mind. The doctor works with bodies. The person who gives massages works with bodies too. The farmer works with land. The wise person's job is to handle their impressions correctly — the way nature intended. Every soul naturally agrees with truth and disagrees with lies. When something is unclear, the soul stays uncertain. The soul naturally wants good things and avoids bad things. When something is neither good nor bad, the soul doesn't care either way. Think of a banker — he can't refuse Caesar's money. Neither can someone selling vegetables. If you show them the coin, they have to accept it and give you what you're buying, whether they want to or not. The soul works the same way. When something truly good appears, it immediately attracts the soul. Evil repels it. The soul will never reject something that's clearly good, just like people won't reject Caesar's coin. This principle drives everything both humans and gods do.

discourses_what-is-the-matter-on-which-a.originalText: Against (or with respect to) this kind of thing chiefly a man should exercise himself. As soon as you go out in the morning, examine every man whom you see, every man whom you hear; answer as to a question, What have you seen? A handsome man or woman? Apply the rule. Is this independent of the will, or dependent? Independent. Take it away. What have you seen? A man lamenting over the death of a child. Apply the rule. Death is a thing independent of the will. Take it away. Has the proconsul met you? Apply the rule. What kind of a thing is a proconsul's office? Independent of the will or dependent on it? Independent. Take this away also; it does not stand examination; cast it away; it is nothing to you.
discourses_what-is-the-matter-on-which-a.plainEnglish: This is the main thing you should practice. The moment you step outside in the morning, look at everyone you see and hear. Ask yourself: What did I just see? A good-looking man or woman? Use the rule. Is this up to you or not? It's not up to you. Dismiss it. What did you see? Someone crying over their dead child? Use the rule. Death is not up to you. Dismiss it. Did you run into a government official? Use the rule. What is a government position? Is it up to you or not? It's not up to you. Dismiss this too. It doesn't pass the test. Throw it out. It's nothing to you.

discourses_what-is-the-matter-on-which-a.originalText: If we practised this and exercised ourselves in it daily from morning to night, something indeed would be done. But now we are forthwith caught half asleep by every appearance, and it is only, if ever, that in the school we are roused a little. Then when we go out, if we see a man lamenting, we say, He is undone. If we see a consul, we say, He is happy. If we see an exiled man, we say, He is miserable. If we see a poor man, we say, He is wretched; he has nothing to eat.
discourses_what-is-the-matter-on-which-a.plainEnglish: If we practiced this and worked on it every day from morning to night, we'd actually get somewhere. But instead, we get caught off guard by every impression that comes our way. We're half asleep most of the time. Maybe — just maybe — we wake up a little when we're in class. Then we go outside. We see someone crying and think, "He's ruined." We see a government official and think, "He's got it made." We see someone in exile and think, "He's miserable." We see a poor person and think, "He's suffering — he has nothing to eat."

discourses_what-is-the-matter-on-which-a.originalText: We ought then to eradicate these bad opinions, and to this end we should direct all our efforts. For what is weeping and lamenting? Opinion. What is bad fortune? Opinion. What is civil sedition, what is divided opinion, what is blame, what is accusation, what is impiety, what is trifling? All these things are opinions, and nothing more, and opinions about things independent of the will, as if they were good and bad. Let a man transfer these opinions to things dependent on the will, and I engage for him that he will be firm and constant, whatever may be the state of things around him. Such as is a dish of water, such is the soul. Such as is the ray of light which falls on the water, such are the appearances. When the water is moved, the ray also seems to be moved, yet it is not moved. And when then a man is seized with giddiness, it is not the arts and the virtues which are confounded, but the spirit (the nervous power) on which they are impressed; but if the spirit be restored to its settled state, those things also are restored.
discourses_what-is-the-matter-on-which-a.plainEnglish: We need to get rid of these bad opinions. That's where all our effort should go. What is crying and complaining? Just opinion. What is bad luck? Opinion. What are riots, arguments, blame, accusations, disrespect, or petty concerns? All of these are just opinions — nothing more. They're opinions about things outside your control, as if those things were good or bad. Let someone shift these opinions to things within their control, and I promise you they'll stay steady no matter what happens around them. Think of a bowl of water with light shining on it. Your soul is like that water. The things that happen to you are like the light ray hitting the water. When you shake the water, the light ray looks like it's moving too, but it's not really moving. When someone gets dizzy and confused, their skills and character don't actually get scrambled — it's just the mind they're written on that gets shaken up. Once the mind settles down, everything else settles back into place too.

discourses_miscellaneous.originalText: When some person asked him how it happened that since reason has been more cultivated by the men of the present age, the progress made in former times was greater. In what respect, he answered, has it been more cultivated now, and in what respect was the progress greater then? For in that in which it has now been more cultivated, in that also the progress will now be found. At present it has been cultivated for the purpose of resolving syllogisms, and progress is made. But in former times it was cultivated for the purpose of maintaining the governing faculty in a condition conformable to nature, and progress was made. Do not then mix things which are different, and do not expect, when you are laboring at one thing to make progress in another. But see if any man among us when he is intent upon this, the keeping himself in a state conformable to nature and living so always, does not make progress. For you will not find such a man.
discourses_miscellaneous.plainEnglish: Someone asked Epictetus: "Why did people make more progress in the old days, when we've gotten so much better at reasoning now?" He answered: "Better at what kind of reasoning? And what kind of progress are you talking about? You'll make progress in whatever you actually work on. Today we use reasoning to solve logical puzzles, and sure enough, we get good at that. But back then, people used reasoning to keep their minds in harmony with nature, and they got good at that. Don't mix up different goals. Don't expect to get better at one thing when you're working on something else entirely. Show me someone today who focuses on living according to nature — really focuses on it — and I'll show you someone making real progress. But you won't find anyone like that."

discourses_miscellaneous.originalText: It is not easy to exhort weak young men; for neither is it easy to hold (soft) cheese with a hook. But those who have a good natural disposition, even if you try to turn them aside, cling still more to reason.
discourses_miscellaneous.plainEnglish: It's not easy to encourage weak young men. You can't hold soft cheese with a hook. But those with good character will stick to reason even more when you try to pull them away from it.

discourses_to-the-administrator-of-the-f.originalText: When the administrator came to visit him, and the man was an Epicurean, Epictetus said, It is proper for us who are not philosophers to inquire of you who are philosophers, as those who come to a strange city inquire of the citizens and those who are acquainted with it, what is the best thing in the world, in order that we also after inquiry may go in quest of that which is best and look at it, as strangers do with the things in cities. For that there are three things which relate to man—soul, body, and things external, scarcely any man denies. It remains for you philosophers to answer what is the best. What shall we say to men? Is the flesh the best? and was it for this that Maximus sailed as far as Cassiope in winter (or bad weather) with his son, and accompanied him that he might be gratified in the flesh? When the man said that it was not, and added, Far be that from him. Is it not fit then, Epictetus said, to be actively employed about the best? It is certainly of all things the most fit. What then do we possess which is better than the flesh? The soul, he replied. And the good things of the best, are they better, or the good things of the worse? The good things of the best.
discourses_to-the-administrator-of-the-f.plainEnglish: An administrator came to visit Epictetus. The man was an Epicurean. Epictetus said to him: "We who aren't philosophers should ask you philosophers what's best in life. It's like strangers visiting a new city — they ask the locals what's worth seeing. Everyone agrees that humans have three parts: soul, body, and external things. So you philosophers need to tell us — which is best? Should we tell people that flesh is the best thing? Is that why Maximus sailed all the way to Cassiope in winter with his son — just so the boy could satisfy his physical desires?" The man said no, that wasn't right at all. "Well then," Epictetus said, "shouldn't we focus our efforts on whatever is truly best? That makes the most sense of all, right? So what do we have that's better than flesh?" "The soul," the man replied. "And are the good things that belong to the best part better than the good things that belong to the worse part?" "Yes, the good things of the best part are better."

discourses_to-the-administrator-of-the-f.originalText: And are the good things of the best within the power of the will or not within the power of the will? They are within the power of the will. Is then the pleasure of the soul a thing within the power of the will? It is, he replied. And on what shall this pleasure depend? On itself? But that cannot be conceived; for there must first exist a certain substance or nature ([Greek: ousia]) of good, by obtaining which we shall have pleasure in the soul. He assented to this also. On what then shall we depend for this pleasure of the soul? for if it shall depend on things of the soul, the substance (nature) of the good is discovered; for good cannot be one thing, and that at which we are rationally delighted another thing; nor if that which precedes is not good, can that which comes after be good, for in order that the thing which comes after may be good, that which precedes must be good. But you would not affirm this, if you are in your right mind, for you would then say what is inconsistent both with Epicurus and the rest of your doctrines.
