I'll be jolted awake by nightmares, disturbed, trembling at every bit of news. My peace of mind will depend on other people's letters.

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: Some person has arrived from Rome. I only hope there is no harm. But what harm can happen to you, where you are not? From Hellas (Greece) some one is come; I hope that there is no harm. In this way every place may be the cause of misfortune to you. Is it not enough for you to be unfortunate there where you are, and must you be so even beyond sea, and by the report of letters? Is this the way in which your affairs are in a state of security? Well then suppose that my friends have died in the places which are far from me. What else have they suffered than that which is the condition of mortals? Or how are you desirous at the same time to live to old age, and at the same time not to see the death of any person whom you love? Know you not that in the course of a long time many and various kinds of things must happen; that a fever shall overpower one, a robber another, and a third a tyrant? Such is the condition of things around us, such are those who live with us in the world; cold and heat, and unsuitable ways of living, and journeys by land, and voyages by sea, and winds, and various circumstances which surround us, destroy one man, and banish another, and throw one upon an embassy and another into an army. Sit down then in a flutter at all these things, lamenting, unhappy, unfortunate, dependent on another, and dependent not on one or two, but on ten thousands upon ten thousands.
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish:
Someone has arrived from Rome. I just hope nothing bad has happened. But what harm can touch you when you're not even there? Someone comes from Greece — I hope nothing's wrong there either. This way, every place becomes a source of worry for you. Isn't it enough to be miserable where you actually are? Do you have to be miserable about distant places too, based on rumors and letters? Is this what you call living securely?

So suppose my friends have died in faraway places. What have they experienced except what all mortals experience? How can you want to live to old age while also expecting never to see anyone you love die? Don't you know that over a long life, many different things must happen? Fever will kill one person, a robber another, a tyrant a third. This is how things are around us. This is the world we live in.

Cold and heat kill people. Bad living conditions kill people. Travel by land and sea kills people. Winds and countless other circumstances destroy one person, exile another, send one on a mission and another to war. So go ahead — sit there in a panic about all these things. Cry and complain. Be miserable and helpless. Make yourself dependent on others — not just one or two people, but thousands upon thousands.

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: Did you hear this when you were with the philosophers? did you learn this? do you not know that human life is a warfare? that one man must keep watch, another must go out as a spy, and a third must fight? and it is not possible that all should be in one place, nor is it better that it should be so. But you neglecting to do the commands of the general complain when anything more hard than usual is imposed on you, and you do not observe what you make the army become as far as it is in your power; that if all imitate you, no man will dig a trench, no man will put a rampart round, nor keep watch, nor expose himself to danger, but will appear to be useless for the purposes of an army. Again, in a vessel if you go as a sailor, keep to one place and stick to it. And if you are ordered to climb the mast, refuse; if to run to the head of the ship, refuse; and what master of a ship will endure you? and will he not pitch you overboard as a useless thing, an impediment only and bad example to the other sailors? And so it is here also: every man's life is a kind of warfare, and it is long and diversified. You must observe the duty of a soldier and do every thing at the nod of the general; if it is possible, divining what his wishes are; for there is no resemblance between that general and this, neither in strength nor in superiority of character.
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish:
Didn't you learn this when you studied philosophy? Don't you know that human life is warfare? One person must stand guard. Another must scout ahead. A third must fight. They can't all be in the same place. And it wouldn't be better if they were.

But you ignore the general's orders. Then you complain when something harder than usual gets assigned to you. You don't see what you're doing to the army. If everyone copies you, no one will dig trenches. No one will build defenses or stand guard or face danger. Everyone will be useless as soldiers.

Same thing on a ship. If you're a sailor, stay at your post. If you're ordered to climb the mast, don't refuse. If you're told to run to the front of the ship, don't refuse. What ship captain would put up with you? He'd throw you overboard as dead weight — just getting in the way and setting a bad example for the other sailors.

It's the same in life. Every person's life is a kind of warfare. It's long and full of different battles. You must do your duty as a soldier. Follow every signal from the general. If you can, figure out what he wants before he asks. This general is nothing like earthly generals. He's far stronger and far superior in character.

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: Know you not that a good man does nothing for the sake of appearance, but for the sake of doing right? What advantage is it then to him to have done right? And what advantage is it to a man who writes the name of Dion to write it as he ought? The advantage is to have written it. Is there no reward then? Do you seek a reward for a good man greater than doing what is good and just? At Olympia you wish for nothing more, but it seems to you enough to be crowned at the games. Does it seem to you so small and worthless a thing to be good and happy? For these purposes being introduced by the gods into this city (the world), and it being now your duty to undertake the work of a man, do you still want nurses also and a mamma, and do foolish women by their weeping move you and make you effeminate? Will you thus never cease to be a foolish child? know you not that he who does the acts of a child, the older he is, the more ridiculous he is?
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish: Don't you know that a good person doesn't act for show? They act because it's right. So what's the benefit of doing right? What's the benefit to someone who writes the name "Dion" correctly? The benefit is that they wrote it correctly. Isn't there a reward then? Are you looking for some reward greater than doing what's good and just? At the Olympics, you don't want anything more than winning. That seems like enough to you. Does being good and happy seem so small and worthless? The gods brought you into this world for these purposes. Now it's your job to do the work of an adult. Do you still want nurses and your mommy? Will you let foolish women make you weak with their crying? Will you never stop being a foolish child? Don't you know that the older someone gets, the more ridiculous they look when they act like a child?

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: So in this matter also: if you kiss your own child, or your brother or friend, never give full license to the appearance ([Greek: phantasian]), and allow not your pleasure to go as far as it chooses; but check it, and curb it as those who stand behind men in their triumphs and remind them that they are mortal. Do you also remind yourself in like manner, that he whom you love is mortal, and that what you love is nothing of your own; it has been given to you for the present, not that it should not be taken from you, nor has it been given to you for all time, but as a fig is given to you or a bunch of grapes at the appointed season of the year. But if you wish for these things in winter, you are a fool. So if you wish for your son or friend when it is not allowed to you, you must know that you are wishing for a fig in winter. For such as winter is to a fig, such is every event which happens from the universe to the things which are taken away according to its nature.
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish: So here's what you should do: when you kiss your child, your brother, or your friend, don't let your feelings run wild. Don't let your pleasure go as far as it wants. Hold it back. Control it. Think of those servants who stand behind generals during victory parades and whisper, "Remember, you are mortal." You should remind yourself the same way. The person you love is mortal. What you love is not really yours. It has been given to you for now — not permanently, and not forever. It's like a fig or grapes given to you in their proper season. If you want figs in winter, you're being foolish. If you want your son or friend when they're no longer available to you, you're wishing for figs in winter. Winter is to figs what death and loss are to the things we love — it's just the natural order.

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: And further, at the times when you are delighted with a thing, place before yourself the contrary appearances. What harm is it while you are kissing your child to say with a lisping voice: To-morrow you will die; and to a friend also: To-morrow you will go away or I shall, and never shall we see one another again? But these are words of bad omen—and some incantations also are of bad omen; but because they are useful, I don't care for this; only let them be useful. But do you call things to be of bad omen except those which are significant of some evil? Cowardice is a word of bad omen, and meanness of spirit, and sorrow, and grief, and shamelessness. These words are of bad omen; and yet we ought not to hesitate to utter them in order to protect ourselves against the things. Do you tell me that a name which is significant of any natural thing is of evil omen?
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish: Here's another exercise: When you're enjoying something, picture the opposite happening. What's the harm in whispering to your child as you kiss them, "Tomorrow you might die"? Or saying to a friend, "Tomorrow you'll leave, or I will, and we'll never see each other again"? You think these are cursed words? Some charms are supposedly cursed too. But if they're useful, I don't care about the superstition. Let them be useful. What do you really call cursed — only things that point to real evil? Cowardice is cursed. So is a weak spirit, sadness, grief, and shamelessness. These words point to cursed things. Yet we shouldn't hesitate to say them out loud to guard ourselves against what they represent. Are you telling me that naming something natural is an evil omen?

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: say that even for the ears of corn to be reaped is of bad omen, for it signifies the destruction of the ears, but not of the world. Say that the falling of the leaves also is of bad omen, and for the dried fig to take the place of the green fig, and for raisins to be made from the grapes. For all these things are changes from a former state into other states; not a destruction, but a certain fixed economy and administration. Such is going away from home and a small change: such is death, a greater change, not from the state which now is to that which is not, but to that which is not now. Shall I then no longer exist? You will not exist, but you will be something else, of which the world now has need; for you also came into existence not when you chose, but when the world had need of you.
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish: People say it's a bad sign when grain is harvested. They think it means destruction of the grain, but not destruction of the world. They say it's bad when leaves fall. Or when dried figs replace fresh ones. Or when grapes become raisins. All these things are just changes from one state to another. They're not destruction. They're part of how the world works and manages itself. Going away from home is like this — a small change. Death is like this too — a bigger change. You don't go from existing to not existing. You go from what you are now to something you're not now. Will I stop existing then? You won't exist as you are now. But you'll be something else that the world needs. You didn't choose when to be born either. You came into existence when the world needed you.

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: Let these thoughts be ready to hand by night and by day; these you should write, these you should read; about these you should talk to yourself and to others. Ask a man: Can you help me at all for this purpose? and further, go to another and to another. Then if anything that is said be contrary to your wish, this reflection first will immediately relieve you, that it is not unexpected. For it is a great thing in all cases to say: I knew that I begot a son who is mortal. For so you also will say: I knew that I am mortal, I knew that I may leave my home, I knew that I may be ejected from it, I knew that I may be led to prison. Then if you turn round and look to yourself, and seek the place from which comes that which has happened, you will forthwith recollect that it comes from the place of things which are out of the power of the will, and of things which are not my own. What then is it to me? Then, you will ask, and this is the chief thing: And who is it that sent it? The leader, or the general, the state, the law of the state. Give it me then, for I must always obey the law in everything.
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish: Keep these thoughts ready all the time — day and night. Write them down. Read them. Talk to yourself about them. Talk to others about them. Ask people: Can you help me with this? Go from person to person asking. When something happens that goes against what you wanted, this thought will immediately comfort you: it's not a surprise. It's a great thing to be able to say in every situation: I knew I had a son who would die someday. You can also say: I knew I would die. I knew I might have to leave my home. I knew I might get kicked out. I knew I might go to prison. When something happens, turn around and look at yourself. Ask where this thing came from. You'll remember right away that it comes from things outside your control — things that aren't really yours. So what is this to me? Then ask yourself the most important question: Who sent this? The leader? The general? The state? The law? Give it to me then. I must always obey the law in everything.

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: Then, when the appearance (of things) pains you, for it is not in your power to prevent this, contend against it by the aid of reason, conquer it: do not allow it to gain strength nor to lead you to the consequences by raising images such as it pleases and as it pleases. If you be in Gyara, do not imagine the mode of living at Rome, and how many pleasures there were for him who lived there and how many there would be for him who returned to Rome; but fix your mind on this matter, how a man who lives in Gyara ought to live in Gyara like a man of courage. And if you be in Rome, do not imagine what the life in Athens is, but think only of the life in Rome.
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish: When things look bad and upset you — and you can't stop that first reaction — fight back with reason. Beat those thoughts. Don't let them grow stronger or drag you into imagining all sorts of terrible scenarios. If you're stuck on some miserable island, don't fantasize about the good life back in Rome — all the pleasures you're missing and could have again if you returned. Instead, focus on this: how should a brave person live on this island? And if you're in Rome, don't daydream about life in Athens. Think only about how to live well in Rome.

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: Then in the place of all other delights substitute this, that of being conscious that you are obeying God, that not in word, but in deed you are performing the acts of a wise and good man. For what a thing it is for a man to be able to say to himself: Now whatever the rest may say in solemn manner in the schools and may be judged to be saying in a way contrary to common opinion (or in a strange way), this I am doing; and they are sitting and are discoursing of my virtues and inquiring about me and praising me; and of this Zeus has willed that I shall receive from myself a demonstration, and shall myself know if he has a soldier such as he ought to have, a citizen such as he ought to have, and if he has chosen to produce me to the rest of mankind as a witness of the things which are independent of the will: See that you fear without reason, that you foolishly desire what you do desire; seek not the good in things external; seek it in yourselves: if you do not, you will not find it.
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish: Instead of chasing other pleasures, find joy in this: knowing you're following God's will. Not just talking about it, but actually living like a wise and good person. What a powerful thing it is to tell yourself: 'Right now, I'm doing what others only discuss in their fancy lectures — things that sound strange or go against popular opinion. They sit around debating my character, asking about me, praising me. But Zeus wanted me to prove something to myself. He wanted me to know if I'm the kind of soldier he needs, the kind of citizen he needs. He chose me to show the rest of humanity something about things beyond our control: Look, you're afraid for no reason. You want things you shouldn't want. Don't look for what's good in external things. Look for it within yourselves. If you don't, you'll never find it.'

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: For this purpose he leads me at one time hither, at another time sends me thither, shows me to men as poor, without authority, and sick; sends me to Gyara, leads me into prison, not because he hates me—far from him be such a meaning, for who hates the best of his servants? nor yet because he cares not for me, for he does not neglect any even of the smallest things; but he does this for the purpose of exercising me and making use of me as a witness to others. Being appointed to such a service, do I still care about the place in which I am, or with whom I am, or what men say about me? and do I not entirely direct my thoughts to God and to his instructions and commands?
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish: For this reason, he moves me around — sometimes here, sometimes there. He shows me to people as poor, powerless, and sick. He sends me to Gyara, puts me in prison. Not because he hates me — God forbid! Who hates their best servant? Not because he doesn't care about me either — he doesn't neglect even the smallest things. He does this to train me and use me as an example for others. Since I'm appointed to this job, why should I worry about where I am? Or who I'm with? Or what people say about me? Shouldn't I focus completely on God and his teachings and commands?

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: Having these things (or thoughts) always in hand, and exercising them by yourself, and keeping them in readiness, you will never be in want of one to comfort you and strengthen you. For it is not shameful to be without something to eat, but not to have reason sufficient for keeping away fear and sorrow. But if once you have gained exemption from sorrow and fear, will there any longer be a tyrant for you, or a tyrant's guard, or attendants on Cæsar? Or shall any appointment to offices at court cause you pain, or shall those who sacrifice in the Capitol on the occasion of being named to certain functions, cause pain to you who have received so great authority from Zeus? Only do not make a proud display of it, nor boast of it; but show it by your acts; and if no man perceives it, be satisfied that you are yourself in a healthy state and happy.
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish: Keep these thoughts always at hand. Practice them by yourself. Have them ready to use. Then you'll never lack something to comfort and strengthen you. It's not shameful to go without food. But it is shameful not to have enough reason to keep fear and sorrow away. Once you're free from sorrow and fear, is there any tyrant left who can control you? Any tyrant's guard? Any of Caesar's attendants? Will missing out on court appointments still hurt you? Will watching others sacrifice at the Capitol when they get certain positions still cause you pain — you who have received such great authority from Zeus? Just don't show off about it or brag. Show it through your actions instead. And if no one notices, be satisfied that you yourself are healthy and happy.

discourses_to-those-who-fall-off-desist-.originalText:
Consider as to the
things which you proposed to yourself at first, which you have secured,
and which you have not; and how you are pleased when you recall to
memory the one, and are pained about the other; and if it is possible,
recover the things wherein you failed. For we must not shrink when we
are engaged in the greatest combat, but we must even take blows. For
the combat before us is not in wrestling and the Pancration, in which
both the successful and the unsuccessful may have the greatest merit,
or may have little, and in truth may be very fortunate or very
unfortunate; but the combat is for good fortune and happiness
themselves. Well then, even if we have renounced the contest in this
matter (for good fortune and happiness), no man hinders us from
renewing the combat again, and we are not compelled to wait for another
four years that the games at Olympia may come again; but as soon as you
have recovered and restored yourself, and employ the same zeal, you may
renew the combat again; and if again you renounce it, you may again
renew it; and if you once gain the victory, you are like him who has
never renounced the combat. Only do not through a habit of doing the
same thing (renouncing the combat), begin to do it with pleasure, and
then like a bad athlete go about after being conquered in all the
circuit of the games like quails who have run away.
discourses_to-those-who-fall-off-desist-.plainEnglish: Think about the goals you set for yourself at the start. Which ones did you achieve? Which ones did you fail at? Notice how remembering your successes makes you feel good, while thinking about your failures brings pain. If you can, go back and work on the things where you failed. We must not back down when we're fighting the most important battle. We have to be willing to take hits. This fight isn't like wrestling or mixed martial arts, where winners and losers might both show great skill or little skill, and might be very lucky or very unlucky. This fight is for good fortune and happiness itself. So what if you've given up on this contest before? No one stops you from jumping back in. You don't have to wait four years for the next Olympics. As soon as you've recovered and gotten your strength back, and you bring the same energy, you can fight again. If you quit again, you can start again. If you finally win, you're like someone who never quit at all. Just don't make quitting a habit that you start to enjoy. Don't be like a bad athlete who gets beaten at every competition and slinks around like a coward.

discourses_to-those-who-fear-want.originalText:
Are you not ashamed at being more cowardly and more mean than fugitive slaves? How do they when they run away leave their masters? on what estates do they depend, and what domestics do they rely on? Do they not after stealing a little, which is enough for the first days, then afterwards move on through land or through sea, contriving one method after another for maintaining their lives? And what fugitive slave ever died of hunger? But you are afraid lest necessary things should fail you, and are sleepless by night. Wretch, are you so blind, and don't you see the road to which the want of necessaries leads?—Well, where does it lead?—to the same place to which a fever leads, or a stone that falls on you, to death. Have you not often said this yourself to your companions? have you not read much of this kind, and written much? and how often have you boasted that you were easy as to death?

Learn then first what are the things which are shameful, and then tell us that you are a philosopher: but at present do not, even if any other man calls you so, allow it.
discourses_to-those-who-fear-want.plainEnglish:
Aren't you ashamed of being more cowardly and pathetic than runaway slaves? When slaves escape, what do they leave behind? What property do they count on? What servants do they have helping them? They steal a little food for the first few days, then figure out how to survive as they go — traveling by land or sea, coming up with one plan after another to stay alive. Has a runaway slave ever starved to death? But you're terrified that you won't have what you need, and you lie awake at night worrying. You fool, are you so blind that you can't see where lacking necessities actually leads? Well, where does it lead? To the same place that fever leads, or a falling stone — to death. Haven't you said this to your friends many times? Haven't you read plenty about this and written about it too? How often have you bragged that you were comfortable with death?

So first learn what things are actually shameful. Then tell us you're a philosopher. But right now, don't call yourself one — even if someone else does.

discourses_to-those-who-fear-want.originalText: Is that shameful to you which is not your own act, that of which you are not the cause, that which has come to you by accident, as a headache, as a fever? If your parents were poor, and left their property to others, and if while they live, they do not help you at all, is this shameful to you? Is this what you learned with the philosophers? Did you never hear that the thing which is shameful ought to be blamed, and that which is blamable is worthy of blame? Whom do you blame for an act which is not his own, which he did not do himself? Did you then make your father such as he is, or is it in your power to improve him? Is this power given to you? Well then, ought you to wish the things which are not given to you, or to be ashamed if you do not obtain them? And have you also been accustomed while you were studying philosophy to look to others and to hope for nothing from yourself?
discourses_to-those-who-fear-want.plainEnglish: Are you really ashamed of something that isn't your fault? Something you didn't cause? Something that just happened to you, like a headache or fever? If your parents were poor and left their money to someone else, if they don't help you while they're alive — are you ashamed of that? Is this what you learned from philosophers? Didn't you ever hear that only blameworthy things should make you ashamed? And that you can only blame people for their own actions? Who do you blame for something they didn't do themselves? Did you make your father who he is? Can you change him? Do you have that power? No. So should you want things you can't have? Should you be ashamed when you don't get them? Have you been studying philosophy just to depend on other people and expect nothing from yourself?

discourses_to-those-who-fear-want.originalText: Lament then and groan and eat with fear that you may not have food to-morrow. Tremble about your poor slaves lest they steal, lest they run away, lest they die. So live, and continue to live, you who in name only have approached philosophy, and have disgraced its theorems as far as you can by showing them to be useless and unprofitable to those who take them up; you, who have never sought constancy, freedom from perturbation, and from passions; you who have not sought any person for the sake of this object, but many for the sake of syllogisms; you who have never thoroughly examined any of these appearances by yourself, Am I able to bear, or am I not able to bear? What remains for me to do? But as if all your affairs were well and secure, you have been resting on the third topic, that of things being unchanged, in order that you may possess unchanged—what? cowardice, mean spirit, the admiration of the rich, desire without attaining any end, and avoidance ([Greek: echchlisin]) which fails in the attempt? About security in these things you have been anxious.
discourses_to-those-who-fear-want.plainEnglish: Go ahead then. Cry and moan and eat in fear that you might not have food tomorrow. Shake with worry about your poor slaves — that they might steal from you, run away, or die. Keep living like this. Keep it up, you who have only touched philosophy in name and have disgraced its teachings as much as you can. You've shown them to be worthless and useless to anyone who tries them. You've never looked for steadiness, peace of mind, or freedom from your emotions. You've never sought out any teacher for these goals — only many teachers for clever arguments. You've never seriously examined any of these situations by asking yourself: Can I handle this, or can't I? What should I do next? Instead, as if everything in your life were fine and safe, you've been focused on the third topic — keeping things unchanged. But what are you trying to keep unchanged? Your cowardice, your small spirit, your worship of rich people, your desires that never get satisfied, and your avoidance that always fails. This is what you've been worried about protecting.

discourses_to-those-who-fear-want.originalText: Ought you not to have gained something in addition from reason, and then to have protected this with security? And whom did you ever see building a battlement all around and encircling it with a wall? And what doorkeeper is placed with no door to watch? But you practise in order to be able to prove—what? You practise that you may not be tossed as on the sea through sophisms, and tossed about from what? Show me first what you hold, what you measure, or what you weigh; and show me the scales or the medimnus (the measure); or how long will you go on measuring the dust? Ought you not to demonstrate those things which make men happy, which make things go on for them in the way as they wish, and why we ought to blame no man, accuse no man, and acquiesce in the administration of the universe?
discourses_to-those-who-fear-want.plainEnglish: Shouldn't reason have given you something more? Shouldn't you protect that something? Have you ever seen someone build a wall around nothing? What good is a guard with no door to watch? But you practice just to prove things — prove what exactly? You practice so arguments won't confuse you — but confuse you about what? First show me what you actually believe. What are you measuring? Show me your scales. How long will you keep measuring dust? You should be proving the things that make people happy. The things that help life go the way they want. Why we shouldn't blame anyone or accuse anyone. Why we should accept how the universe works.

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: He is free who lives as he wishes to live; who is neither subject to compulsion nor to hindrance, nor to force; whose movements to action ([Greek: hormai]) are not impeded, whose desires attain their purpose, and who does not fall into that which he would avoid ([Greek: echchliseis aperiptotoi]). Who then chooses to live in error? No man. Who chooses to live deceived, liable to mistake, unjust, unrestrained, discontented, mean? No man. Not one then of the bad lives as he wishes; nor is he then free. And who chooses to live in sorrow, fear, envy, pity, desiring and failing in his desires, attempting to avoid something and falling into it? Not one. Do we then find any of the bad free from sorrow, free from fear, who does not fall into that which he would avoid, and does not obtain that which he wishes? Not one; nor then do we find any bad man free.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: A free person lives how they want to live. They're not forced, blocked, or pushed around. Their actions flow naturally. They get what they want and avoid what they don't want. So who chooses to live in error? Nobody. Who chooses to live deceived, prone to mistakes, unfair, out of control, unhappy, or petty? Nobody. None of the bad people live as they wish. So they're not free. Who chooses to live in grief, fear, envy, or pity? Who chooses to want things and not get them, or to try avoiding something and fall right into it? Nobody. Do we find any bad people who are free from grief and fear? Any who avoid what they don't want and get what they do want? Not one. So we don't find any bad people who are free.

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: Further, then, answer me this question, also: does freedom seem to you to be something great and noble and valuable? How should it not seem so? Is it possible then when a man obtains anything so great and valuable and noble to be mean? It is not possible. When then you see any man subject to another or flattering him contrary to his own opinion, confidently affirm that this man also is not free; and not only if he do this for a bit of supper, but also if he does it for a government (province) or a consulship; and call these men little slaves who for the sake of little matters do these things, and those who do so for the sake of great things call great slaves, as they deserve to be. This is admitted also. Do you think that freedom is a thing independent and self-governing? Certainly. Whomsoever then it is in the power of another to hinder and compel, declare that he is not free.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: Now answer this: Does freedom seem great and noble and valuable to you? Of course it does. So when someone gets something this great and valuable and noble, can they act like a coward? No way. When you see someone bowing to another person or flattering them against their own beliefs, say confidently that this person is not free. It doesn't matter if they're doing it for a free meal or for a government position or high office. Call the people who do this for small things "little slaves." Call the ones who do it for big things "great slaves" — because that's what they are. You agree with this, right? Do you think freedom means being independent and self-governing? Absolutely. So anyone who can be stopped or forced by another person — declare that they are not free.

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: And do not look, I entreat you, after his grandfathers and great-grandfathers, or inquire about his being bought or sold, but if you hear him saying from his heart and with feeling, "Master," even if the twelve fasces precede him (as consul), call him a slave. And if you hear him say, "Wretch that I am, how much I suffer," call him a slave. If, finally, you see him lamenting, complaining, unhappy, call him a slave, though he wears a praetexta. If, then, he is doing nothing of this kind do not yet say that he is free, but learn his opinions, whether they are subject to compulsion, or may produce hindrance, or to bad fortune, and if you find him such, call him a slave who has a holiday in the Saturnalia; say that his master is from home; he will return soon, and you will know what he suffers.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: Don't worry about someone's family background or whether they were born free or enslaved. Listen to what they actually say. If you hear them calling anyone "Master" from the heart — even if they're a consul with all the official honors — call them a slave. If you hear them saying "Poor me, look how much I suffer," call them a slave. If you see them complaining, whining, or miserable, call them a slave, even if they wear the finest clothes. But if they don't do any of these things, don't assume they're free yet. Check their beliefs. Are their thoughts controlled by outside forces? Can external things mess with their peace of mind? Can bad luck ruin them? If so, call them a slave on vacation — like during Saturnalia when slaves get a brief break. Their master is just away for now. He'll be back soon, and then you'll see what they really endure.

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: What then is that which makes a man free from hindrance and makes him his own master? For wealth does not do it, nor consulship, nor provincial government, nor royal power; but something else must be discovered. What then is that which when we write makes us free from hindrance and unimpeded? The knowledge of the art of writing. What then is it in playing the lute? The science of playing the lute. Therefore in life also it is the science of life. You have then heard in a general way; but examine the thing also in the several parts. Is it possible that he who desires any of the things which depend on others can be free from hindrance? No. Is it possible for him to be unimpeded? No. Therefore he cannot be free. Consider then, whether we have nothing which is in our own power only, or whether we have all things, or whether some things are in our own power, and others in the power of others.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: So what makes a person truly free and in charge of their own life? Money doesn't do it. Neither does being a consul, ruling a province, or having royal power. There must be something else. What makes you free and unblocked when you're writing? Knowing how to write. What about when you're playing the lute? Knowing how to play the lute. So in life, it must be knowing how to live. You've heard this in general terms. But let's look at the details. Can someone who wants things that depend on other people be free from obstacles? No. Can they be unblocked? No. So they can't be free. Think about this: do we have nothing that's completely under our control? Or do we control everything? Or do we control some things while others control other things?

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: What do you mean? When you wish the body to be entire (sound) is it in your power or not? It is not in my power. When you wish it to be healthy? Neither is this in my power. When you wish it to be handsome? Nor is this. Life or death? Neither is this in my power. Your body then is another's, subject to every man who is stronger than yourself. It is. But your estate is it in your power to have it when you please, and as long as you please, and such as you please? No. And your slaves? No. And your clothes? No. And your house? No. And your horses? Not one of these things. And if you wish by all means your children to live, or your wife, or your brother, or your friends, is it in your power? This also is not in my power.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: What do you mean? When you want your body to be whole and sound, is that up to you or not? It's not up to me. When you want it to be healthy? That's not up to me either. When you want it to be attractive? Not that either. Life or death? That's not up to me. So your body belongs to someone else — it's subject to anyone stronger than you. It is. But your property — is it up to you to have it when you want, for as long as you want, exactly as you want? No. And your slaves? No. And your clothes? No. And your house? No. And your horses? Not one of these things. And if you desperately want your children to live, or your wife, or your brother, or your friends — is that up to you? This also is not up to me.

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: Whether then have you nothing which is in your own power, which depends on yourself only and cannot be taken from you, or have you anything of the kind? I know not. Look at the thing then thus, and examine it. Is any man able to make you assent to that which is false? No man. In the matter of assent then you are free from hindrance and obstruction. Granted. Well; and can a man force you to desire to move towards that to which you do not choose? He can, for when he threatens me with death or bonds he compels me to desire to move towards it. If then you despise death and bonds, do you still pay any regard to him? No. Is then the despising of death an act of your own or is it not yours? It is my act.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: Do you have anything that belongs completely to you? Something that depends only on you and can't be taken away? I don't know. Let's look at this and figure it out. Can anyone force you to believe something false? No one can. So when it comes to what you believe, you're free. No one can stop you. Agreed? Good. Now, can someone force you to want something you don't actually want? Yes, he can. When he threatens me with death or prison, he makes me want to move toward what he wants. But what if you don't fear death or prison? Do you still care what he thinks? No. So is not fearing death your own action, or isn't it? It's my own action.

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: When you have made this preparation, and have practised this discipline, to distinguish that which belongs to another from that which is your own, the things which are subject to hindrance from those which are not, to consider the things free from hindrance to concern yourself, and those which are not free not to concern yourself, to keep your desire steadily fixed to the things which do concern yourself, and turned from the things which do not concern yourself; do you still fear any man? No one. For about what will you be afraid? About the things which are your own, in which consists the nature of good and evil? and who has power over these things? who can take them away? who can impede them? No man can, no more than he can impede God. But will you be afraid about your body and your possessions, about things which are not yours, about things which in no way concern you?
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: Once you've prepared yourself and practiced this discipline — separating what belongs to others from what's yours, what can be blocked from what can't be blocked, focusing only on what can't be blocked and ignoring what can be — do you still fear anyone? No. What would you be afraid of? The things that are truly yours, where good and evil actually exist? Who has power over those? Who can take them away or stop them? No one can — any more than they can stop God. But are you going to be afraid about your body and your stuff? Things that aren't really yours? Things that don't actually concern you?

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: and what else have you been studying from the beginning than to distinguish between your own and not your own, the things which are in your power and not in your power, the things subject to hindrance and not subject? and why have you come to the philosophers? was it that you may nevertheless be unfortunate and unhappy? You will then in this way, as I have supposed you to have done, be without fear and disturbance. And what is grief to you? for fear comes from what you expect, but grief from that which is present. But what further will you desire? For of the things which are within the power of the will, as being good and present, you have a proper and regulated desire; but of the things which are not in the power of the will you do not desire any one, and so you do not allow any place to that which is irrational, and impatient, and above measure hasty.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: What else have you been studying all along? You've been learning to tell the difference between what's yours and what's not yours. What's in your power and what's not. What can be blocked and what can't. So why did you come to the philosophers? Was it so you could still be miserable and unhappy? If you do what I'm assuming you've done, you'll be without fear and worry. And what is grief to you then? Fear comes from what you expect to happen. Grief comes from what's happening now. But what more could you want? For the things that are within your control — the good things that are here now — you have proper, well-ordered desires. For the things outside your control, you don't want any of them. So you don't give any room to what's irrational, impatient, and way too hasty.

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: Then after receiving everything from another and even yourself, are you angry and do you blame the giver if he takes anything from you? Who are you, and for what purpose did you come into the world? Did not he (God) introduce you here, did he not show you the light, did he not give you fellow-workers, and perceptions and reason? and as whom did he introduce you here? did he not introduce you as subject to death, and as one to live on the earth with a little flesh, and to observe his administration, and to join with him in the spectacle and the festival for a short time? Will you not then, as long as you have been permitted, after seeing the spectacle and the solemnity, when he leads you out, go with adoration of him and thanks for what you have heard and seen? No; but I would still enjoy the feast. The initiated too would wish to be longer in the initiation; and perhaps also those at Olympia to see other athletes. But the solemnity is ended; go away like a grateful and modest man; make room for others; others also must be born, as you were, and, being born, they must have a place, and houses, and necessary things. And if the first do not retire, what remains? Why are you insatiable? Why are you not content? why do you contract the world? Yes, but I would have my little children with me and my wife.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: You've received everything from someone else — even your own self. So why do you get angry and blame the giver when he takes something back from you? Who are you? What are you here for? Didn't God bring you into this world? Didn't he show you the light? Didn't he give you people to work alongside, and senses, and the ability to think? And what did he make you? He made you mortal. He put you on earth with a little bit of flesh. You're here to watch how he runs things and to join in his show and celebration for a short time. When your time is up and he calls you to leave, won't you go with respect and gratitude for everything you've seen and heard? No — you say you want to keep enjoying the party. People at religious ceremonies would also like to stay longer. People at the Olympic games would like to see more athletes compete. But the ceremony is over. Leave like a grateful and humble person. Make room for others. Other people need to be born, just like you were. And once they're born, they need space and homes and the things they require. If the first people never leave, what's left for the rest? Why can't you ever have enough? Why aren't you satisfied? Why are you trying to squeeze the world tight? 'But I want my children and my wife with me.'

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: What, are they yours? do they not belong to the giver, and to him who made you? then will you not give up what belongs to others? will you not give way to him who is superior? Why then did he introduce me into the world on these conditions? And if the conditions do not suit you, depart. He has no need of a spectator who is not satisfied. He wants those who join in the festival, those who take part in the chorus, that they may rather applaud, admire, and celebrate with hymns the solemnity. But those who can bear no trouble, and the cowardly, he will not unwillingly see absent from the great assembly ([Greek: panaeguris]) for they did not when they were present behave as they ought to do at a festival nor fill up their place properly, but they lamented, found fault with the deity, fortune, their companions; not seeing both what they had, and their own powers, which they received for contrary purposes, the powers of magnanimity, of a generous mind, manly spirit, and what we are now inquiring about, freedom. For what purpose then have I received these things? To use them. How long? So long as he who has lent them chooses. What if they are necessary to me? Do not attach yourself to them and they will not be necessary; do not say to yourself that they are necessary, and then they are not necessary.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: What, are these things yours? Don't they belong to whoever gave them to you and made you? Then why won't you give up what belongs to others? Why won't you step aside for someone who's superior? "But why did he bring me into the world under these conditions?" If you don't like the conditions, leave. He doesn't need a spectator who complains. He wants people who join the celebration, who take part in the chorus, who applaud and admire and sing praises for the occasion. But those who can't handle any trouble, the cowards — he won't mind if they skip the great gathering. When they were there, they didn't act like they should at a festival. They didn't fill their role properly. Instead they whined, complained about God, about fortune, about their companions. They couldn't see what they had or their own powers, which they received for the opposite purpose — powers of courage, generosity, strong spirit, and what we're talking about now: freedom. So why did I receive these things? To use them. For how long? As long as whoever lent them decides. "But what if I need them?" Don't attach yourself to them and you won't need them. Don't tell yourself they're necessary, and then they won't be necessary.

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: You then, a man may say, are you free? I wish, by the gods, and pray to be free; but I am not yet able to face my masters, I still value my poor body, I value greatly the preservation of it entire, though I do not possess it entire. But I can point out to you a free man, that you may no longer seek an example. Diogenes was free. How was he free? Not because he was born of free parents, but because he was himself free, because he had cast off all the handles of slavery, and it was not possible for any man to approach him, nor had any man the means of laying hold of him to enslave him. He had everything easily loosed, everything only hanging to him. If you laid hold of his property, he would have rather let it go and be yours, than he would have followed you for it; if you had laid hold of his leg, he would have let go his leg; if of all his body, all his poor body; his intimates, friends, country, just the same. For he knew from whence he had them, and from whom, and on what conditions.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: You might ask me, "Are you free then?" I wish I were, and I pray to be free. But I'm not there yet. I can't face my masters. I still value this poor body of mine. I care deeply about keeping it intact, even though I don't truly own it. But I can show you someone who was free, so you don't have to keep looking for an example. Diogenes was free. How was he free? Not because his parents were free, but because he made himself free. He threw off everything that could enslave him. No one could get close enough to grab him and make him a slave. Everything he had was loose in his grip, barely attached to him. If you grabbed his possessions, he would have let them go rather than chase after you. If you grabbed his leg, he would have let go of his leg. If you took his whole body, his whole poor body — fine. Same with his close friends, his buddies, his country. He knew where all these things came from, who gave them to him, and under what conditions.

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: His true parents indeed, the gods, and his real country he would never have deserted, nor would he have yielded to any man in obedience to them and to their orders, nor would any man have died for his country more readily. For he was not used to inquire when he should be considered to have done anything on behalf of the whole of things (the universe, or all the world), but he remembered that everything which is done comes from thence and is done on behalf of that country and is commanded by him who administers it. Therefore see what Diogenes himself says and writes: "For this reason," he says, "Diogenes, it is in your power to speak both with the King of the Persians and with Archidamus the King of the Lacedaemonians, as you please." Was it because he was born of free parents? I suppose all the Athenians and all the Lacedaemonians, because they were born of slaves, could not talk with them (these kings) as they wished, but feared and paid court to them. Why then does he say that it is in his power? Because I do not consider the poor body to be my own, because I want nothing, because law is everything to me, and nothing else is. These were the things which permitted him to be free.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: His true parents were the gods, and his real country was the universe. He would never abandon them. He obeyed them more than anyone else. No one would die for his country more willingly. He didn't question when he was serving the whole universe. He remembered that everything comes from there and serves that country, commanded by whoever runs it. So look at what Diogenes himself says: "This is why, Diogenes, you can speak to the King of Persia and to King Archidamus of Sparta however you want." Was this because he had free parents? I guess all Athenians and Spartans, born from slaves, couldn't talk to these kings as they wished. They were afraid and sucked up to them instead. So why does he say he has this power? "Because I don't think this poor body belongs to me. Because I want nothing. Because law is everything to me, and nothing else matters." These things made him free.

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: Think of these things, these opinions, these words; look to these examples, if you would be free, if you desire the thing according to its worth. And what is the wonder if you buy so great a thing at the price of things so many and so great? For the sake of this which is called liberty, some hang themselves, others throw themselves down precipices, and sometimes even whole cities have perished; and will you not for the sake of the true and unassailable and secure liberty give back to God when he demands them the things which he has given? Will you not, as Plato says, study not to die only, but also to endure torture, and exile, and scourging, and, in a word, to give up all which is not your own? If you will not, you will be a slave among slaves, even if you be ten thousand times a consul; and if you make your way up to the palace (Cæsar's residence), you will no less be a slave; and you will feel that perhaps philosophers utter words which are contrary to common opinion (paradoxes), as Cleanthes also said, but not words contrary to reason.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: Think about these ideas, these beliefs, these words. Look at these examples if you want to be free — if you really want freedom for what it's worth. Why be surprised that something so valuable costs so much? People have hanged themselves for what they call liberty. Others have thrown themselves off cliffs. Sometimes entire cities have died for it. So why won't you give back to God what he gave you when he asks for it — all for true, unshakeable, secure freedom? Why won't you do what Plato says: learn not just to die, but to endure torture, exile, beatings — in short, to give up everything that isn't really yours? If you won't do this, you'll be a slave among slaves. Even if you become consul ten thousand times. Even if you make it to Caesar's palace. You'll still be a slave. And you'll realize that maybe philosophers say things that go against popular opinion — paradoxes, as Cleanthes called them — but not things that go against reason.

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: For you will know by experience that the words are true, and that there is no profit from the things which are valued and eagerly sought to those who have obtained them; and to those who have not yet obtained them there is an imagination ([Greek: phantasia]), that when these things are come, all that is good will come with them; then, when they are come, the feverish feeling is the same, the tossing to and fro is the same, the satiety, the desire of things, which are not present; for freedom is acquired not by the full possession of the things which are desired, but by removing the desire. And that you may know that this is true, as you have labored for those things, so transfer your labor to these: be vigilant for the purpose of acquiring an opinion which will make you free; pay court to a philosopher instead of to a rich old man; be seen about a philosopher's doors; you will not disgrace yourself by being seen; you will not go away empty nor without profit, if you go to the philosopher as you ought, and if not (if you do not succeed), try at least; the trial (attempt) is not disgraceful.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish:
You'll learn from experience that these words are true. The things people value and chase after don't actually benefit those who get them. And for those who don't have them yet, there's this fantasy that once they get these things, everything good will come with them. But when they finally get them, the restless feeling is still there. The tossing and turning is still there. The dissatisfaction is still there. The wanting what you don't have is still there. You don't get freedom by fully possessing the things you want. You get it by removing the wanting itself. 

To prove this is true, put the same effort into philosophy that you put into chasing those other things. Stay alert to develop beliefs that will make you free. Court a philosopher instead of some rich old man. Be seen hanging around a philosopher's door. You won't embarrass yourself by being seen there. You won't leave empty-handed or without gain — if you approach the philosopher the right way. And if you don't succeed, at least try. The attempt itself is not shameful.

discourses_on-familiar-intimacy.originalText:
To this matter before all you must attend, that
you be never so closely connected with any of your former intimates or
friends as to come down to the same acts as he does. If you do not
observe this rule, you will ruin yourself. But if the thought arises in
your mind, “I shall seem disobliging to him and he will not have the
same feeling towards me,” remember that nothing is done without cost,
nor is it possible for a man if he does not do the same things to be
the same man that he was. Choose then which of the two you will have,
to be equally loved by those by whom you were formerly loved, being the
same with your former self; or, being superior, not to obtain from your
friends the same that you did before.
discourses_on-familiar-intimacy.plainEnglish: Pay attention to this above all else: never get so close to old friends that you sink down to their level and do what they do. If you ignore this rule, you'll destroy yourself. You might think, "But I'll seem unfriendly to him, and he won't like me as much." Remember that nothing comes free. You can't do different things and still be the same person you were before. So choose: Do you want to be loved the same way by the same people, staying exactly who you used to be? Or do you want to become better, knowing your friends might not treat you the same way they used to?

discourses_what-things-we-should-exchang.originalText: Keep this thought in readiness, when you lose anything external, what you acquire in place of it; and if it be worth more, never say, I have had a loss; neither if you have got a horse in place of an ass, or an ox in place of a sheep, nor a good action in place of a bit of money, nor in place of idle talk such tranquillity as befits a man, nor in place of lewd talk if you have acquired modesty. If you remember this, you will always maintain your character such as it ought to be.
discourses_what-things-we-should-exchang.plainEnglish: Keep this thought ready: when you lose something external, ask what you gain instead. If what you gain is worth more, never say you've suffered a loss. You wouldn't say that if you got a horse instead of a donkey, or an ox instead of a sheep. Same goes for getting a good deed instead of money, or proper calm instead of pointless chatter, or modesty instead of crude talk. Remember this, and you'll always keep your character where it should be.

discourses_what-things-we-should-exchang.originalText: But if you do not, consider that the times of opportunity are perishing, and that whatever pains you take about yourself, you are going to waste them all and overturn them. And it needs only a few things for the loss and overturning of all—namely, a small deviation from reason. For the steerer of a ship to upset it, he has no need of the same means as he has need of for saving it; but if he turns it a little to the wind, it is lost; and if he does not do this purposely, but has been neglecting his duty a little, the ship is lost. Something of the kind happens in this case also; if you only fall a nodding a little, all that you have up to this time collected is gone.
discourses_what-things-we-should-exchang.plainEnglish: If you don't pay attention, remember this: your chances are slipping away. Whatever effort you've put into improving yourself will be wasted and destroyed. It takes very little to lose everything you've worked for — just a tiny slip from sound thinking. A ship's captain doesn't need much to wreck his vessel. He needs skill and effort to save it, but to destroy it? He just has to turn the wheel slightly into the wind. The ship is lost. He doesn't even have to do it on purpose — a moment of carelessness is enough. It's the same with your progress. Nod off just a little, and everything you've built up disappears.

discourses_what-things-we-should-exchang.originalText: Attend therefore to the appearances of things, and watch over them; for that which you have to preserve is no small matter, but it is modesty and fidelity and constancy, freedom from the affects, a state of mind undisturbed, freedom from fear, tranquillity, in a word liberty. For what will you sell these things? See what is the value of the things which you will obtain in exchange for these.—But shall I not obtain any such thing for it?—See, and if you do in return get that, see what you receive in place of it. I possess decency, he possesses a tribuneship: he possesses a prætorship, I possess modesty. But I do not make acclamations where it is not becoming: I will not stand up where I ought not; for I am free, and a friend of God. and so I obey him willingly. But I must not claim (seek) anything else, neither body nor possession, nor magistracy, nor good report, nor in fact anything. For he (God) does not allow me to claim (seek) them, for if he had chosen, he would have made them good for me; but he has not done so, and for this reason I cannot transgress his commands. Preserve that which is your own good in everything; and as to every other thing, as it is permitted, and so far as to behave consistently with reason in respect to them, content with this only. If you do not, you will be unfortunate, you will fail in all things, you will be hindered, you will be impeded. These are the laws which have been sent from thence (from God); these are the orders. Of these laws a man ought to be an expositor, to these he ought to submit, not to those of Masurius and Cassius.
discourses_what-things-we-should-exchang.plainEnglish: Pay attention to how things appear to you. Watch over your thoughts carefully. What you're protecting isn't small — it's your self-respect, your trustworthiness, your consistency, your emotional calm, your peace of mind, your freedom from fear, your inner quiet. In short, your liberty. What would you sell these things for? Look at what you think you'd get in return. "But won't I get something good for it?" Look closely. If you do get something back, see what you're actually receiving. I have decency, he has a government position. He has a judgeship, I have self-respect. But I don't cheer where it's inappropriate. I won't stand up where I shouldn't. I'm free and a friend of God, so I obey him willingly. But I can't demand anything else — not my body, possessions, political office, good reputation, or anything else. God doesn't let me demand these things. If he wanted them to be good for me, he would have made them so. Since he hasn't, I can't go against his commands. Protect what is truly your own good in everything. As for everything else, handle it as you're allowed to, and only as far as reason permits. Be content with this. If you don't, you'll be miserable. You'll fail at everything. You'll be blocked and obstructed. These are the laws sent from above. These are the orders. You should interpret these laws and submit to them — not to the laws of Masurius and Cassius.

discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.originalText: Remember that not only the desire of power and of riches makes us mean and subject to others, but even the desire of tranquillity, and of leisure, and of travelling abroad, and of learning. For, to speak plainly, whatever the external thing may be, the value which we set upon it places us in subjection to others. What then is the difference between desiring to be a senator or not desiring to be one; what is the difference between desiring power or being content with a private station; what is the difference between saying, I am unhappy, I have nothing to do, but I am bound to my books as a corpse; or saying, I am unhappy, I have no leisure for reading? For as salutations and power are things external and independent of the will, so is a book. For what purpose do you choose to read? Tell me. For if you only direct your purpose to being amused or learning something, you are a silly fellow and incapable of enduring labor. But if you refer reading to the proper end, what else is this than a tranquil and happy life ([Greek: eusoia])?
discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.plainEnglish: Remember that it's not just wanting power and money that makes us weak and dependent on others. Even wanting peace, free time, travel, and learning can do the same thing. To be honest, whatever external thing you care about puts you at the mercy of others. So what's the difference between wanting to be a senator and not wanting to be one? What's the difference between craving power and being happy with private life? What's the difference between saying "I'm miserable, I have nothing to do, I'm chained to my books like a dead body" and saying "I'm miserable, I have no time to read"? Praise and power are external things beyond your control. So is a book. Why do you want to read? Tell me. If you're just reading to have fun or learn random facts, you're foolish and can't handle real work. But if you read for the right reason, what is that reason other than living a calm and happy life?

discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.originalText: But if reading does not secure for you a happy and tranquil life, what is the use of it? But it does secure this, the man replies, and for this reason I am vexed that I am deprived of it.—And what is this tranquil and happy life, which any man can impede, I do not say Cæsar or Cæsar's friend, but a crow, a piper, a fever, and thirty thousand other things? But a tranquil and happy life contains nothing so sure as continuity and freedom from obstacle. Now I am called to do something: I will go then with the purpose of observing the measures (rules) which I must keep, of acting with modesty, steadiness, without desire and aversion to things external; and then that I may attend to men, what they say, how they are moved; and this not with any bad disposition, or that I may have something to blame or to ridicule; but I turn to myself, and ask if I also commit the same faults. How then shall I cease to commit them? Formerly I also acted wrong, but now I do not: thanks to God.
discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.plainEnglish: But if reading doesn't give you a happy and peaceful life, what's the point? "But it does give me that," someone says, "and that's why I'm upset when I can't read." — But what kind of peaceful and happy life can be blocked by anyone — not just Caesar or his friends, but a crow, a flute player, a fever, or any of thirty thousand other things? A truly peaceful and happy life has nothing more reliable than staying steady and being free from obstacles. Now I'm called to do something. I'll go with the plan to follow the rules I need to keep. I'll act with humility, steadiness, without wanting or avoiding external things. Then I can pay attention to other people — what they say and how they react. I won't do this with bad intentions, or to find something to criticize or make fun of. Instead, I turn to myself and ask: do I make the same mistakes? How can I stop making them? I used to act badly too, but now I don't. Thanks to God.

discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.originalText: What then is the reason of this? The reason is that we have never read for this purpose, we have never written for this purpose, so that we may in our actions use in a way conformable to nature the appearances presented to us; but we terminate in this, in learning what is said, and in being able to expound it to another, in resolving a syllogism, and in handling the hypothetical syllogism. For this reason where our study (purpose) is, there alone is the impediment. Would you have by all means the things which are not in your power? Be prevented then, be hindered, fail in your purpose.
discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.plainEnglish: So why does this happen? Because we never read or write with the right goal in mind. We don't study so we can handle life's situations naturally and wisely. Instead, we stop at just learning what the books say. We focus on explaining ideas to others, solving logical puzzles, and working through hypothetical arguments. That's why we get stuck exactly where we put our attention. Do you insist on wanting things that aren't up to you? Then expect to be blocked, frustrated, and disappointed.

discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.originalText: But if we read what is written about action (efforts, [Greek: hormae]), not that we may see what is said about action, but that we may act well; if we read what is said about desire and aversion (avoiding things), in order that we may neither fail in our desires, nor fall into that which we try to avoid; if we read what is said about duty (officium), in order that remembering the relations (of things to one another) we may do nothing irrationally nor contrary to these relations; we should not be vexed, in being hindered as to our readings, but we should be satisfied with doing the acts which are conformable (to the relations), and we should be reckoning not what so far we have been accustomed to reckon: To-day I have read so many verses, I have written so many; but (we should say), To-day I have employed my action as it is taught by the philosophers; I have not employed my desire; I have used avoidance ([Greek: echchlisei]) only with respect to things which are within the power of my will; I have not been afraid of such a person, I have not been prevailed upon by the entreaties of another; I have exercised my patience, my abstinence, my co-operation with others; and so we should thank God for what we ought to thank him.
discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.plainEnglish: But what if we read about action not just to see what's written, but to actually act well? What if we read about desire and aversion so we get what we want and avoid what we don't want? What if we read about duty so we remember how things relate to each other and act rationally? Then we wouldn't get upset when something interrupts our reading. We'd be happy doing what's right. And we wouldn't keep score the old way: "Today I read this many pages, I wrote this much." Instead we'd say: "Today I acted the way philosophers teach. I controlled my desires. I only avoided things that are actually up to me. I wasn't afraid of that person. I didn't give in to someone's begging. I practiced patience, self-control, and cooperation." That's what we should thank God for.

discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.originalText: There is only one way to happiness, and let this rule be ready both in the morning and during the day and by night: the rule is not to look towards things which are out of the power of our will, to think that nothing is our own, to give up all things to the Divinity, to Fortune; to make them the superintendents of these things, whom Zeus also has made so; for a man to observe that only which is his own, that which cannot be hindered; and when we read, to refer our reading to this only, and our writing and our listening. For this reason I cannot call the man industrious, if I hear this only, that he reads and writes; and even if a man adds that he reads all night, I cannot say so, if he knows not to what he should refer his reading. For neither do you say that a man is industrious if he keeps awake for a girl, nor do I. But if he does it (reads and writes) for reputation, I say that he is a lover of reputation. And if he does it for money, I say that he is a lover of money, not a lover of labor; and if he does it through love of learning, I say that he is a lover of learning. But if he refers his labor to his own ruling power that he may keep it in a state conformable to nature and pass his life in that state, then only do I say that he is industrious.
discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.plainEnglish: There's only one path to happiness. Keep this rule ready morning, noon, and night: Don't focus on things outside your control. Think that nothing truly belongs to you. Give everything up to God, to fortune. Let them manage what Zeus has put them in charge of. You should only pay attention to what is truly yours — what cannot be taken from you. When you read, connect it only to this principle. Same with your writing and listening. This is why I won't call someone hardworking just because they read and write. Even if someone reads all night, I won't call them hardworking if they don't know why they're reading. You wouldn't call a man hardworking for staying up all night for a woman, would you? Neither would I. If he reads for reputation, he loves reputation. If he does it for money, he loves money — not work itself. If he does it for learning, he loves learning. But if he connects his work to his inner self — to keep it aligned with nature and live that way — only then do I call him truly industrious.

discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.originalText: For never commend a man on account of these things which are common to all, but on account of his opinions (principles); for these are the things which belong to each man, which make his actions bad or good. Remembering these rules, rejoice in that which is present, and be content with the things which come in season. If you see anything which you have learned and inquired about occurring to you in your course of life (or opportunely applied by you to the acts of life), be delighted at it. If you have laid aside or have lessened bad disposition and a habit of reviling; if you have done so with rash temper, obscene words, hastiness, sluggishness; if you are not moved by what you formerly were, and not in the same way as you once were, you can celebrate a festival daily, to-day because you have behaved well in one act, and to-morrow because you have behaved well in another. How much greater is this a reason for making sacrifices than a consulship or the government of a province? These things come to you from yourself and from the gods. Remember this, who gives these things and to whom, and for what purpose. If you cherish yourself in these thoughts, do you still think that it makes any difference where you shall be happy, where you shall please God? Are not the gods equally distant from all places? Do they not see from all places alike that which is going on?
discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.plainEnglish: Don't praise people for things everyone has in common. Praise them for their principles. Those are what belong to each person. Those are what make their actions good or bad. Keep these rules in mind. Be happy with what you have right now. Be content with what comes when it's supposed to come. If you see something you've learned showing up in your life, be delighted. If you've gotten rid of bad habits or made them weaker — bad temper, cruel words, rashness, dirty language, impatience, laziness — if you're not moved by the same things that used to bother you, or not in the same way, you can celebrate every day. Today because you acted well in one situation. Tomorrow because you acted well in another. This is a much better reason to celebrate than getting elected consul or governing a province. These improvements come from you and from the gods. Remember this. Remember who gives these gifts, to whom, and why. If you keep these thoughts close, do you really think it matters where you are when you're happy? Where you are when you please God? Aren't the gods equally far from all places? Don't they see everything that's happening from everywhere?

discourses_against-the-quarrelsome-and-f.originalText: The wise and good man neither himself fights with any person, nor does he allow another, so far as he can prevent it. And an example of this as well as of all other things is proposed to us in the life of Socrates, who not only himself on all occasions avoided fights (quarrels), but would not allow even others to quarrel. See in Xenophon's Symposium how many quarrels he settled, how further he endured Thrasymachus and Polus and Callicles; how he tolerated his wife, and how he tolerated his son who attempted to confute him and to cavil with him. For he remembered well that no man has in his power another man's ruling principle. He wished therefore for nothing else than that which was his own. And what is this?
discourses_against-the-quarrelsome-and-f.plainEnglish: A wise and good person doesn't fight with anyone. He also stops others from fighting when he can. Socrates shows us how to do this. He avoided arguments himself and wouldn't let other people argue either. Look at Xenophon's Symposium. See how many fights Socrates stopped. See how he put up with Thrasymachus, Polus, and Callicles. See how he tolerated his wife and his son, even when his son tried to argue with him and criticize him. Socrates remembered something important: you can't control another person's mind. So he only wanted what was actually his own. What is that?

discourses_against-the-quarrelsome-and-f.originalText: Not that this or that man may act according to nature, for that is a thing which belongs to another; but that while others are doing their own acts, as they choose, he may nevertheless be in a condition conformable to nature and live in it, only doing what is his own to the end that others also may be in a state conformable to nature. For this is the object always set before him by the wise and good man. Is it to be commander (a prætor) of an army? No; but if it is permitted him, his object is in this matter to maintain his own ruling principle. Is it to marry?
